articles.title_original: Thermal Management of Film Capacitors Using Graphene/Thermoplastic Polyurethane Composite Films
articles.title_en: Graphene/TPU Composite Films Improve Film-Capacitor Thermal Management
articles.excerpt_original: Thermal management is important for improving the safety, reliability, and service life of film capacitors operating under high-power conditions. In this study, graphene/thermoplastic polyurethane (TPU) composite films were prepared for capacitor heat dissipation. Physically modified graphene (G1) and chemically modified graphene (G2) were incorporated into TPU at loadings of 0.03, 0.06, and 0.30 wt%. The structural characteristics and chemical states of the films were investigated using X-ray diffraction (XRD), Raman spectroscopy, Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FT-IR), and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS). The thermal conductivity and thermal diffusivity of the composite films were evaluated, and a numerical model was used to investigate their effect on capacitor thermal behavior. The results showed that graphene incorporation preserved the major chemical structure of the TPU matrix while modifying its structural and surface chemical characteristics. The thermal response depended on both graphene type and loading. Among the tested samples, the 0.06 wt% G1/TPU film exhibited the highest measured thermal conductivity of 0.236 W/(m∙K). The thermal diffusivity showed a nonmonotonic dependence on graphene loading, with the maximum values obtained at 0.06 wt% graphene. Numerical results indicated that the thermally conductive film improved heat-flux uniformity and reduced the temperature gradient within the capacitor model. These findings demonstrate the potential of graphene/TPU composite films as flexible thermal-interface materials for capacitor thermal management.

articles.title_original: Advanced N-Graphene-Based Electromagnetic Shields via Microwave Plasma Induced Synthesis
articles.title_en: Plasma-Synthesized N-Doped Graphene Nanocomposites Enable Broadband EM Shielding
articles.excerpt_original: Here, a plasma-enabled strategy is presented for the controllable fabrication of ultralight nanocomposites with absorption-dominated EM-shielding performance across the 5–70 GHz frequency range. The fabricated nanocomposites exhibit average microwave absorption exceeding 60% across the 5–25 GHz frequency range and 70% across the 25–70 GHz range while maintaining a constant thickness of 2 mm and a fixed filler content of 15 wt%. Plasma-driven nanoscale engineering and multiphase hybridization synergistically enhance dielectric and magnetic loss mechanisms, resulting in effective absorption bandwidths in the C-band (2.1 GHz), Ku-band (3.4 GHz), Ka-band (8 GHz) and V-band (4 GHz). The plasma process produces free-standing nitrogen-doped graphene sheets uniformly decorated with FexOy, MnOx, and TiOx nanoparticles, which are subsequently incorporated into a polymer matrix. The microwave plasma environment simultaneously enables graphene nanosheet synthesis, metal oxide nanoparticles formation, surface functionalization, multiphase generation, and the anchoring of nanoparticles onto the graphene scaffold. Using low-cost precursors such as acetonitrile and micron-sized metal oxides, the process achieves production rates of up to 50 mg min−1. Overall, this one-step plasma-enabled approach provides a low-cost, scalable, and efficient route for manufacturing lightweight, high-performance EM wave absorbers.

articles.title_original: Graphene-Based Photodetectors for Silicon Photonic Optical Communications: Progress, Challenges, and Outlook
articles.title_en: Graphene Photodetectors Advance High-Speed Silicon Photonics
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Graphene-based photodetectors have emerged as an interesting alternative to conventional semiconductor photodiodes for integrated silicon photonic systems. This perspective reviews the evolution of waveguide-integrated graphene photodetectors from their first demonstrations in 2013 to recent devices achieving responsivities up to 0.65 A/W and bandwidths exceeding 180 GHz, with experimentally proven potential to surpass 500 GHz. These advances highlight graphene’s unique potential for ultrahigh-speed optical communication and microwave photonic applications. We discuss the underlying photodetection mechanisms, key performance metrics, and integration strategies that enable efficient coupling between graphene and silicon photonic waveguides. Despite impressive progress, graphene photodetectors currently do not surpass state-of-the-art germanium photodiodes in responsivity, noise-equivalent power, or manufacturing maturity. Consequently, graphene is unlikely to replace established technologies in standard telecom receivers in the coming years. Instead, its greatest impact is expected in applications requiring extreme bandwidth, broadband wavelength operation, and heterogeneous integration across diverse photonic platforms.
articles.summary_en: A perspective reviews graphene photodetectors integrated with silicon waveguides, reporting responsivities up to 0.65 A/W and bandwidths above 180 GHz, with potential beyond 500 GHz. It concludes that graphene is unlikely to replace germanium photodiodes in standard telecom receivers soon but may serve extreme-bandwidth and broadband photonic applications.

articles.title_original: rGO-MXene 2D Interfacial Engineering for Enhanced Efficiency and Stability of Perovskite Solar Cells and Modules

articles.excerpt_original: Abstract In this work, we report an innovative interface engineering strategy combining bidirectional chemical anchoring and electronic bridging via a 2D reduced graphene oxide (rGO) and MXene conductive network. This hierarchical 2D structure suppresses the aggregation and stacking of single-layer MXene nanosheets while mutually compensating for individual charge transport limitations. Specifically, the abundant functional groups passivate interfacial defects (Pb2+ and I–) and bond with the PCBM layer via coordination, hydrogen bonding and π–π interactions. This synergistic architecture lowers the electron energy offset. Consequently, PSCs incorporating the rGO-MXene interlayer achieve a champion power conversion efficiency (PCE) of 25.96% (certified 25.05%) and retain 96.43% of initial efficiency after 1000 h in ambient air. Furthermore, 10 × 10 cm2 large-area PSM yields a high PCE of 20.25%, maintaining 96.05% of initial efficiency under maximum power point tracking for 963 h.

articles.title_original: High-Efficiency Desalination with MXene Membranes via Tailored Surface Terminations and Nanochannel Architectures
articles.title_en: MXene Membrane Design Improves Desalination Selectivity
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Freshwater scarcity has driven growing interest in MXene membranes for seawater desalination. However, improving the trade-off between water permeability and ion selectivity remains a key challenge. In this study, we investigated the performance of MXene membranes for seawater desalination via reverse osmosis through molecular dynamics simulations. Specifically, the impacts of layer number, slit geometry, and surface terminations on separation efficiency were systematically evaluated. Our results revealed that a trilayer misaligned slit geometry markedly increased ion rejection, compared with their bilayer and monolayer counterparts. Furthermore, we also identified a key synergy in the desalination process between geometric confinement and surface chemistry. A mixed-termination strategy could overcome conventional performance limits, which combined hydrophilic hydroxyl (−OH) termination with electronegative fluorine (−F) and oxygen (−O) terminations. The −OH terminations enhanced water permeability by lowering the free-energy barrier. In contrast, the other two terminations (−F, −O) achieved complete ion rejection through strong electrostatic repulsion. Consequently, a trilayer misaligned MXene membrane with mixed terminations achieved a favorable balance between flux and selectivity. These molecular-level insights provide qualitative guidance for regulating terminal groups and slit geometry in MXene nanochannels, thereby offering the design of more efficient and practical desalination membranes.
articles.summary_en: Molecular dynamics simulations show that trilayer, misaligned MXene nanochannels with mixed surface terminations can improve the trade-off between water permeability and ion rejection. Hydroxyl groups promote water transport, while fluorine and oxygen terminations enhance ion exclusion, offering design guidance for desalination membranes.

articles.title_original: 0D/2D PbS/1T‐CrS 2 Heterostructure for High‐Performance Ultraviolet to Near‐Infrared Detection
articles.title_en: PbS/1T-CrS₂ Heterostructure Enables High-Performance Broadband Photodetection
articles.excerpt_original: ABSTRACT Zero‐dimensional (0D) lead sulfide (PbS) quantum dots (QDs), with their size‐tunable bandgaps, hold great promise for high‐efficiency photodetection across a broad spectral range. However, the presence of surface ligands on colloidal PbS QDs and their inherently isolated states hinder efficient carrier transport. In contrast, two‐dimensional (2D) materials such as metallic 1T‐phase CrS 2 , which are free of dangling bonds, can serve as highly effective carrier transport channel. Here, a strategy for constructing high‐performance photodetectors based on ligand‐free PbS QDs, achieved by converting a PbI 2 film into PbS QDs on a novel 2D metallic 1T‐CrS 2 layer, is proposed. By combining the metallic character of 1T‐CrS 2 with the strong optical responsivity of 0D PbS QDs and theoretically predicted low‐resistance contact at the PbS‐QDs/1T‐CrS 2 interface, this research demonstrates a stable broadband photodetector with outstanding performance such as responsivity (95.1 A/W@1550 nm and 2.7 A/W@375 nm) and a sub‐millisecond response time (0.31 ms@1550 nm and 0.69 ms@375 nm). This heterostructure utilizes the 0D PbS QDs as the photoactive layer and 1T‐CrS 2 as an efficient carrier transport medium, synergistically enhancing the overall photodetection performance. This study opens a new avenue for designing high‐performance, broadband photodetectors leveraging quantum dot‐2D material heterostructures.

Comprehensive structural and physicochemical analyses confirmed the generation of highly crystalline perovskite oxides and their successful integration with g‐C 3 N 4 . LaCoO 3 /g‐C 3 N 4 (LCO/GCN) displayed superior optoelectronic and electrochemical properties, exhibiting the highest electrocatalytic activity toward AA oxidation with good selectivity, excellent reproducibility, operational cycling stability over 100 cycles, and successful applicability to real vitamin C samples analyses.

articles.title_original: High-Speed Energy-Efficient Resonant Modulator on a Graphene-Organic Hybrid Platform
articles.title_en: Graphene–Organic Hybrid Modulator Reaches 320 Gbit/s
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Resonant electro-optic modulators are of interest for encoding electrical signals to the optical domain with an option to perform simultaneous wavelength-division multiplexing while reducing the modulation energy consumption. Here, we demonstrate a compact, high-speed, and energy-efficient resonant modulator exploiting the ultrafast characteristics of graphene and organic materials, enabling efficient electro-optic modulation on the silicon platform. Graphene, with its extraordinary electronic and optical properties, is used as a transparent electrode material that brings the radio frequency field close to the photonic mode with minimal extra losses, while the organic material provides a high linear electro-optic coefficient. This arrangement provides both efficient light modulation in a compact device with an active length of 50 μm and a large modulation bandwidth of ∼35 GHz. High-speed data transmission experiments demonstrate a line rate of 320 Gbit/s, while a rate of 128 Gbit/s is achieved under CMOS-compatible voltages with energy consumption of ∼10.1 femtojoules per bit. The presented technology offers a practical and promising route toward integration of graphene into high-speed communication links.

articles.title_original: Controlled Interfacial Electronic Coupling in Chemical Vapor Deposition-Grown WSe2 Monolayers on Au(111)
articles.title_en: Interface Engineering Tunes Electronic Coupling in WSe2 Monolayers
articles.excerpt_original: We report on the controlled growth and interface engineering of high-quality WSe2 monolayers on Au(111) using ambient-pressure chemical vapor deposition (CVD) combined with comprehensive surface-sensitive characterization in ultrahigh vacuum (UHV). The as-grown films exhibit a selenium buffer layer, which enables the formation of a weakly coupled WSe2 phase at the metal interface, as revealed by scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) and low-energy electron diffraction (LEED). Annealing in UHV removes the selenium buffer layer and leads to the emergence of a pronounced moiré superstructure and a transition toward a strongly coupled WSe2 phase. Furthermore, this transformation is accompanied by pronounced modifications of the electronic structure, including phase-dependent changes in the valence band structure observed by angle-resolved photoelectron spectroscopy (ARPES), a hybridization-induced metallization measured by scanning tunneling spectroscopy (STS), and a significant decrease in the work function determined by field emission resonance (FER) and ultraviolet photoemission spectroscopy (UPS). Density functional theory (DFT) calculations confirm strong WSe2-Au hybridization and the presence of the mid-gap states for the strongly coupled phase, whereas the Se8 buffer layer weakens the interaction of WSe2 with Au, so that its electronic structure is close to that for the freestanding system. Our results demonstrate that growth-induced interface chemistry provides a powerful handle to tune the electronic coupling in WSe2/Au(111), establishing a direct link between interfacial structure and electronic properties in metal-transition metal dichalcogenide (TMD) interfaces.
articles.summary_en: Researchers controlled the coupling between CVD-grown WSe2 monolayers and Au(111) by using and removing a selenium buffer layer. The resulting changes in hybridization, metallization, work function, and electronic structure provide a route to tuning metal–TMD interfaces for semiconductor applications.

articles.title_original: In Situ Electric Tuning―An Emerging STM Tactic for Probing Exotic Quantum Materials
articles.title_en: In Situ Electric Tuning Advances STM Probing of Graphene Quantum Materials
articles.excerpt_original: ABSTRACT In situ electric tuning (ISET) integrated with scanning tunneling microscopy and spectroscopy (STM/STS) has established itself as a highly effective methodology for controlling quantum electronic states in low‐dimensional materials. This approach combines the sub‐atomic spatial resolution and meV‐resolved spectroscopic capability of STM with the reversible and continuously tunable carrier modulation of field‐effect device architectures. To date, this approach has been applied to numerous systems, including graphene‐based van der Waals heterostructures, correlated electron systems, and moiré superlattice systems hosting emergent quantum phases. Herein, we systematically summarize the state‐of‐the‐art experimental implementations, including global electrostatic gating, tip‐induced local gating, tip‐induced voltage pulse, and in‐plane electric tuning, accompanied with distinct physics under each configuration. We then highlight key representative advances in resolving gate‐dependent band renormalization, correlated insulating states, charge ordering, symmetry breaking, and electrically driven metastable phases at the nanoscale. We discuss practical limitations, such as restricted carrier‐density ranges, tip‐induced perturbations, dielectric reliability, and challenges in decoupling electric effects from current injection and Joule heating. Looking forward, we outline future directions in device engineering, including programmable local electrostatics, scalable architectures, and integrated platforms for operando studies, highlighting their potential to enable deterministic control of emergent quantum phases in functional materials.
articles.summary_en: A review examines in situ electric tuning combined with scanning tunneling microscopy and spectroscopy to control and study electronic states in graphene-based heterostructures and moiré systems. It identifies advances in nanoscale measurements while noting limitations including carrier-density range, dielectric reliability, and Joule heating.

articles.title_original: A Review of Antimicrobial Mechanisms of Graphene Oxide, Reduced Graphene Oxide, and Graphene Nanoplatelets: Implications for Polymer-Based Dental Materials
articles.title_en: Review Assesses Antimicrobial Graphene Materials for Dental Polymers
articles.excerpt_original: Graphene-based materials, including graphene oxide (GO), reduced graphene oxide (rGO), and graphene nanoplatelets (GNPs), exhibit a relatively large surface area and tunable surface chemistry, enabling diverse biological interactions. These interactions depend on oxygen-containing functional groups, oxidation degree, lateral size, and surface charge. In dental materials, these properties support incorporation of graphene-based materials into polymer matrices to reduce microbial adhesion, inhibit biofilm formation, and limit infection-related degradation. This review critically evaluates GO, rGO, and GNPs in polymer-based dental materials, focusing on structure–property–biological response relationships and antimicrobial performance. Current evidence indicates that GO demonstrates the most consistent antibacterial and antifungal activity, mainly due to its high density of functional groups and hydrophilicity. In contrast, rGO and GNPs show more variable or moderate antimicrobial effects, often requiring surface modification, optimized composite design, or higher material loading. Here, key limitations affecting clinical application are also discussed. Several biological effects are concentration-dependent, including human cytotoxicity, host enzyme interactions, potential immune responses, long-term biocompatibility, and stability under oral conditions. By integrating mechanistic insights across graphene-based materials, this review clarifies their potential and current limitations for polymeric dental applications and identifies priorities supporting the transition from laboratory-scale research to clinical and industrial implementation strategies.
articles.summary_en: A review examines how graphene oxide, reduced graphene oxide, and graphene nanoplatelets can reduce microbial adhesion, biofilm formation, and infection-related degradation in polymer-based dental materials. It highlights graphene oxide’s more consistent antimicrobial activity while noting concentration-dependent cytotoxicity, biocompatibility, stability, and clinical translation challenges.

articles.title_original: Graphene-based nanomaterials in biosensing: current advances, challenges, and future directions for precision diagnostics
articles.title_en: Review assesses graphene nanomaterials for precision biosensing
articles.excerpt_original: BACKGROUND: Graphene-based nanomaterials (GBNs), including graphene oxide, reduced graphene oxide, graphene quantum dots, and their composites, combine ultra-high surface area, superior conductivity, and tunable optical properties, making them powerful materials for ultra-sensitive biosensing. AIM AND SCOPE: Unlike earlier descriptive, platform-specific surveys, this review is organised around structure-property-performance relationships and applies a uniform critical lens to the primary literature. METHODS: We examine optical (fluorescence, surface plasmon resonance, colorimetric, SERS), electrochemical, and field-effect transistor (FET) biosensors. We compare them head-to-head on sensitivity, reproducibility, scalability, and clinical readiness. KEY FINDINGS: GBN platforms detect pathogens such as SARS-CoV-2, cancer biomarkers, metabolites, and environmental toxins with high sensitivity and selectivity. However, many reported ultra-low detection limits are extrapolated from buffer calibrations rather than measured, and they are rarely validated in blinded clinical cohorts. Some are also physically implausible given the number of target molecules in the assay volume. CHALLENGES: Key barriers are cytotoxicity, non-specific binding, irreproducible synthesis, and regulatory validation. For FETs specifically, the main obstacles are Debye screening, baseline drift, and poor wafer-scale yield. CONCLUSIONS: AI-assisted signal processing, wearable and implantable devices, and 3D-printed multi-analyte lab-on-a-chip systems are critical future directions. Addressing these challenges through interdisciplinary effort could make GBN biosensors a foundation for personalized, point-of-care healthcare.
articles.summary_en: A review evaluates graphene-based nanomaterial biosensors across optical, electrochemical and FET platforms, highlighting sensitivity alongside challenges in clinical validation, reproducibility, cytotoxicity and scale-up. It identifies AI-assisted processing, wearable and implantable devices, and 3D-printed lab-on-chip systems as future directions.

Nonetheless, the relatively low specific energy of conventional electrode materials remains a major obstacle to their widespread commercialization. In this context, polymers and graphene-derived electrode materials have gained substantial consideration owing to their complementary physicochemical characteristics. Conducting polymers (CPs), which include polyaniline (PANI), poly(3,4-ethylenedioxythiophene) (PEDOT), polypyrrole (PPy), and polythiophene (PTh) derivatives, and hypercross-linked polymers (HCPs) offer high pseudocapacitance through reversible redox reactions, whereas graphene and its derivatives provide extraordinary electrical conductivity, higher specific surface area (SSA), outstanding mechanical strength, and excellent chemical durability. The synergistic integration of these materials into polymer/graphene composites has begun as an efficient approach to overcome the intrinsic limitations of individual components and significantly improve electrochemical behavior. articles.title_original: Antibacterial Activity and Surface Wettability of MXene-Functionalized Titanium Implant Surfaces: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
articles.title_en: Review assesses MXene coatings for antibacterial titanium implants
articles.excerpt_original: This systematic review and meta-analysis aims to evaluate the effects of MXene-containing surface modifications and coatings on the antibacterial activity and surface wettability of titanium-based implant surfaces. Titanium and its alloys are widely used in dental and orthopedic implants; however, bacterial colonization and the need to optimize surface properties remain important challenges. MXenes, a family of two-dimensional transition metal carbides, nitrides, and carbonitrides, have emerged as promising materials for surface functionalization owing to their distinctive physicochemical properties and potential biological applications. The review will systematically identify and synthesize evidence from in vitro experimental studies investigating MXene-containing coatings or surface modifications applied to commercially pure titanium or titanium alloy substrates, compared with equivalent MXene-free surfaces. The primary outcomes will be antibacterial activity, assessed by colony-forming unit (CFU) counting, and surface wettability, assessed by water contact angle measurements. Secondary outcomes will include cytocompatibility and electrochemical corrosion behavior. Eligible studies will be critically evaluated for methodological quality, and meta-analyses will be performed when sufficient and comparable quantitative data are available. The findings are expected to provide a comprehensive understanding of the effects of MXene functionalization on titanium implant surfaces, identify limitations in the existing evidence, and support future research on advanced surface engineering strategies for dental and orthopedic implant applications.
articles.summary_en: A systematic review and meta-analysis will evaluate MXene-functionalized titanium implant surfaces for antibacterial activity and wettability. It will also examine cytocompatibility and corrosion behavior in dental and orthopedic applications.

articles.title_original: MXene-polydopamine-cyanobacteria photobioelectrochemical biosensor for atrazine detection in environmental waters
articles.title_en: MXene–Polydopamine–Cyanobacteria Biosensor Detects Atrazine in Water
articles.excerpt_original: A cyanobacteria-based photobioelectrochemical biosensor was developed for the first time using Synechococcus elongatus whole cells immobilized on a Ti₃C₂Tₓ MXene electrode modified with an electropolymerized polydopamine (PDA) layer. This surface created a biotic-abiotic interface that facilitated light-driven electron transfer for the sensitive screening of photosystem II (PSII)-inhibiting herbicides in environmental waters, using atrazine (ATZ) as a model analyte. The biosensor was characterized by scanning electron microscopy (SEM), electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS), X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), and Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR). The detection strategy relies on the inhibition of PSII photosynthetic activity, which produces a concentration-dependent decrease in photocurrent. Under optimized conditions, the biosensor achieved a limit of detection (LOD) of 1.92 nM (0.414 ppb), a linear range of 5-200 nM, and a sensitivity of 177.71 nA decade⁻¹ cm⁻². Interference studies demonstrated class selectivity toward PSII-inhibiting herbicides (e.g., DCMU, simazine, desethylatrazine), with negligible response (< 10%) from non-PSII pesticides and common inorganic ions. Regarding operational stability, the device retained > 95% for 1 day and approximately 93% at day 2. However, a 61% signal loss was observed by day 5 (stored at 4 °C), highlighting an operational limitation inherent to whole-cell biological systems. The biosensor was successfully applied to determine ATZ in groundwater, river water, and seawater, delivering accurate recoveries (99.75-103.9%) and offering a green alternative for on-site environmental monitoring.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a whole-cell photobioelectrochemical biosensor using Ti₃C₂Tₓ MXene, polydopamine and cyanobacteria to detect atrazine in environmental waters. It achieved a 1.92 nM detection limit and accurate measurements in groundwater, river water and seawater, but showed substantial signal loss after five days.

articles.title_original: Defect-interface synergistic engineering of Bi 2 Te 3– x @MXene anodes toward fast-charging and durable sodium storage
articles.title_en: MXene–Bi₂Te₃₋ₓ Anode Enables Fast, Durable Sodium-Ion Storage
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Metal tellurides are promising anode candidates for high-energy sodium-ion batteries (SIBs) owing to their multielectron redox chemistry, but their practical deployment is limited by sluggish reaction kinetics and severe structural instability associated with repeated conversion/alloying reactions. Herein, a Te-vacancy-rich Bi2Te3-x@MXene heterostructure is rationally constructed via synergistic electrostatic assembly and in situ tellurization. Strong Ti-Te interfacial coupling immobilizes Bi2Te3-x nanoparticles on conductive MXene nanosheets, generating a robust three-dimensional architecture with continuous electron/ion transport pathways and enhanced tolerance to volume variation. Meanwhile, Te-vacancy engineering tailors the electronic structure and creates abundant active sites, synergistically accelerating Na⁺ transport kinetics. Combined electrochemical analysis and in situ/ex situ characterizations reveal a highly reversible insertion-conversion-alloying mechanism with stabilized phase evolution during cycling. Consequently, the Bi2Te3-x@MXene anode delivers outstanding rate capability and ultralong cycling stability, retaining 324.8 mAh g-1 after 2000 cycles at 2 A g-1 and maintaining 317.9 mAh g-1 even at 10 A g-1. Moreover, the Na3V2(PO4)3//Bi2Te3-x@MXene full cell achieves a high energy density of 210.6 Wh kg-1 and preserves 104.7 Wh kg-1 even at an ultrahigh power density of 11300 W kg-1. This work highlights the effectiveness of integrating defect chemistry with heterointerface engineering to unlock fast and durable sodium storage in metal tellurides for high-energy and high-power SIBs.
articles.summary_en: Researchers engineered a tellurium-vacancy-rich Bi₂Te₃₋ₓ/MXene heterostructure with strong interfacial coupling, improving electron and ion transport while limiting structural degradation. articles.title_original: Breaking the SS- I on trade-off in 2D TFETs through an isolated conduction band in monolayer AgSe
articles.title_en: Monolayer AgSe TFETs combine sub-60 mV/decade switching with high current
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Tunneling field-effect transistors (TFETs), operating through the band-to-band tunneling (BTBT) mechanism, are widely regarded as strong contenders for future low-power (LP) electronic applications on account of the potential to achieve subthreshold swings (SS) below 60 mV∙dec −1 . Nevertheless, the inherently limited on-state current ( I on ) has consistently posed a significant challenge. Here, we demonstrate that a two-dimensional monolayer AgSe TFET can obtain a sub-60 mV∙dec −1 SS and a high on-current at the same time without complex source engineering strategies. The unique isolated conduction band of monolayer AgSe produces a sharp band edge, significantly enhancing the BTBT efficiency and facilitates steep switching characteristics. For a 10 nm p -type AgSe TFET, an SS as low as 31 mV∙dec −1 is obtained, with on-currents reaching 1617 and 716 μ A∙ μ m −1 for high-performance and LP applications, satisfying the requirements defined by the International Technology Roadmap for Semiconductors. Even if the supply voltage ( V dd ) drops to 0.5 V, the 5 nm device maintains an SS min = 43 mV∙dec −1 , demonstrating excellent voltage scalability. Benchmark comparisons with other widely studied 2D materials further confirm the superior performance of AgSe TFETs. These results identify monolayer AgSe as a highly promising channel material and suggest that isolated-band engineering provides an effective design paradigm for next-generation LP nanoelectronic devices.
articles.summary_en: Researchers report that monolayer AgSe tunneling field-effect transistors could achieve steep subthreshold swings and high on-currents through an isolated conduction band. articles.title_original: Fractional thermal memory effects in a rotating magneto-photo-thermoelastic anisotropic fiber-reinforced semiconductor half-space within the framework of modified photo-thermoelasticity
articles.title_en: Fractional Thermal Memory Model Advances Semiconductor Thermoelastic Analysis
articles.excerpt_original: This work develops a mathematical framework to investigate a rotating anisotropic fiber-reinforced semiconductor half-space subjected to optical excitation and an external magnetic field while incorporating fractional thermal memory effects. The proposed model is formulated within the modified photo-thermoelasticity theory, allowing the coupled interactions among thermal, mechanical, carrier-diffusion, and electromagnetic fields to be analyzed in a unified framework. The heat-conduction equation is generalized using a fractional-order thermal operator, and the resulting dimensionless governing equations are solved analytically through the normal-mode technique combined with an eigenvalue-based approach. Silicon is considered for numerical implementation, and the effects of the fractional-order parameter, rotational speed, and magnetic-field intensity on temperature, carrier concentration, displacement, and stress distributions are examined. The results demonstrate that fractional thermal memory significantly influences wave propagation and energy transport, while rotation and magnetic loading markedly modify the mechanical response through inertia and magnetoelastic coupling. The proposed model provides useful insights into coupled multiphysical processes relevant to advanced semiconductor and optoelectronic applications.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a mathematical model of coupled thermal, mechanical, carrier-diffusion and electromagnetic effects in a rotating, anisotropic, fiber-reinforced semiconductor under optical and magnetic excitation. Silicon-based simulations indicate that fractional thermal memory, rotation and magnetic fields significantly affect energy transport, wave propagation and stress responses.

articles.title_original: Tracing the film structure of an organic semiconductor with photoemission orbital tomography
articles.title_en: Photoemission tomography traces structural changes in organic semiconductor films
articles.excerpt_original: Photoemission orbital tomography (POT) is a powerful tool for investigating the orbitals and electronic band structure of oriented layers of organic molecules. In many cases, POT allows conclusions to be drawn regarding the geometric structure, but so far it has been mainly applied to (sub)monolayers and rarely to bilayers, raising the question of whether POT can also provide structure information for thicker films. Here, we use POT to analyze the band dispersion in up to eight layers of $α$-sexithiophene (6T) adsorbed on Cu(110)-p($2\times1$)O. This linear oligomer turns out to be a textbook example that exemplifies the concepts of intra- and intermolecular band dispersion in molecules. Moreover, the rich band and orbital structure information available from POT for this system enables us to trace subtle changes in the crystal structure as a function of layer thickness. Specifically, we find that the periodicity of an intermolecular band changes with film thickness, revealing an increase of the intralayer distance between the molecules with the number of layers. At the same time, the momentum distribution of photoemission from the highest occupied molecular orbital of 6T discloses a decrease of the molecular tilt angle. Following the evolution of tilt angle and lattice constant with layer thickness, we observe -- purely based on electronic structure data -- that the surface-templated monolayer structure relaxes into the structure of bulk 6T crystals. The experimental findings agree well with the results of density functional theory calculations.
articles.summary_en: Researchers used photoemission orbital tomography and density functional theory to track electronic and structural changes in up to eight layers of α-sexithiophene on oxidized Cu(110). Here, electrochemically exfoliated graphene (EEG) is decorated with surfactant-free gold nanoparticles (AuNPs) through a simple one-pot synthesis that uses only water, sodium hydroxide and glycerol, all inexpensive and green reagents. The AuNPs grow directly on the graphene surface. Base concentration governs particle size, whereas the Au/EEG ratio controls loading with only minor changes in size, allowing the two parameters to be tuned almost independently. The resulting composite reaches an Au loading of 20 wt%, to our knowledge among the highest reported for surfactant-free AuNPs on EEG. In the ethanol oxidation reaction, it outperformed physically mixed, sequentially deposited and ligandstabilized controls, combining the highest mass activity with the lowest Tafel slope and the largest electrochemically active surface area. As a proof-of-concept tryptophan sensor, it oxidized the analyte at 0.57 V, to our knowledge the lowest overpotential reported for this amino acid, with a linear response from 1 to 100 µM, a detection limit of 0.4 µM and good tolerance to common electroactive interferents. articles.excerpt_original: The escalating power density of electronics demands thermal interface materials (TIMs) that simultaneously offer high thermal conductivity, strong adhesion, and environmental sustainability. Conventional thermally conductive adhesives (TCAs) face inherent trade-offs among these properties, often relying on non-recyclable thermosets. Here, we present a sustainable thermoplastic TCA composed of a poly(lipoic acid) (polyLA)-based dynamic polymer matrix integrated with polyvinylpyrrolidone-modified hexagonal boron nitride (BN@PVP). The polyLA matrix incorporates catechol moieties and reversible Fe3+-carboxyl/catechol coordination bonds, creating a dynamically reconfigurable network. This design yields an adhesive (LD50Fe100) with high toughness (1.52 MJ m-3), and strong lap shear adhesion (884 kPa on PMMA and 1210 kPa on steel). The dynamic bonds enable room-temperature self-healing (93.1% efficiency) and robust recyclability. At a BN@PVP loading of 40 wt %, the composite (BN@LD50Fe100) achieves a thermal conductivity of 1.2 W m-1 K-1 while maintaining enhanced mechanical properties. LED chip heat dissipation experiments demonstrate a 4 °C lower operating temperature compared to devices without a TIM, with stable thermal performance over multiple cycles. This work provides a promising material strategy to overcome the traditional trade-offs in TCAs, offering a path toward repairable, reusable, and efficient thermal management solutions for advanced electronic packaging.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a recyclable, self-healing thermoplastic thermal interface adhesive using poly(lipoic acid) and modified boron nitride. The composite achieved 1.2 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹ thermal conductivity and reduced LED operating temperature by 4 °C, supporting advanced electronic packaging.

articles.title_original: Membrane-induced eggshell biomineralization towards controllable crystallization
articles.title_en: Biomimetic membrane enables controlled crystallization and water softening
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract The avian eggshell is an extreme example of rapid biomineralization, yet how its underlying substrate, the eggshell membrane (ESM), initiates this process remains elusive, and the application potential of this fundamental biological mechanism has yet to be explored. Across the 33 avian species examined, ESMs consistently promoted CaCO3 crystallization under standardized in vitro conditions and exhibited low heterogeneous nucleation barriers. Inspired by this mechanism, we designed a biomimetic fibrous membrane (b-FM) that reproduces the structural and chemical features of natural ESMs. The b-FM achieves a deposition rate of 0.58 mg cm−2 day−1, surpassing the fastest natural ESM (0.46 mg cm−2 day−1). This efficiency arises from a threefold synergistic mechanism: (1) strong negative surface potential promoting Ca2⁺ accumulation, (2) reduced heterogeneous nucleation energy barrier, and (3) regulated crystallization pathways. Demonstrating its application potential, a b-FM/glass fiber mesh (b-FM/GF) composite module was employed for water softening in a circulating cooling-water system. In a 30-day continuous circulation experiment, the b-FM/GF-treated system maintained softened water quality and effectively suppressed pipe scaling, with less than 2% reduction in the effective pipe area. These findings reveal shared features of ESM-promoted mineralization and establish design principles for industrial crystallization control.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a fibrous membrane inspired by eggshell membranes that accelerates calcium carbonate deposition through surface-charge and nucleation effects. A membrane–glass fiber module maintained softened cooling water and limited pipe scaling to less than 2% area loss over 30 days.

articles.title_original: Nonlinear Conductive Materials for Adaptive Electric Overstress Control: Theory, Tailoring and Applications
articles.title_en: Review Examines Nonlinear Conductive Materials for Adaptive Electrical Protection
articles.excerpt_original: ABSTRACT Artificial intelligence computing, renewable energy integration and transportation electrification are driving electrical and electronic equipment towards higher power densities, higher voltage ratings and greater miniaturisation. Under these trends, insulation systems have become a key bottleneck for reliability and compactness. Conventional approaches, including enhancing the dielectric strength of uniform materials and geometric‐field grading, are approaching their limits because of trade‐offs between performance and processability, as well as sensitivity to manufacturing tolerances and long‐term parameter drift. In this context, nonlinear conductivity materials (NCMs) provide a promising solution by enabling self‐adaptive electric‐field grading through field‐dependent conductivity, thereby suppressing local field concentrations while maintaining low leakage current under normal operation. This review summarises recent progress in NCMs, focusing on conduction mechanisms, property‐tailoring strategies and representative applications. Furthermore, this review also highlights critical scientific and technological challenges in material design and engineering implementation. Addressing these hurdles is essential for establishing NCMs as a robust, enabling solution for the next generation of intelligent, miniaturised and high‐performance electrical and electronic devices.
articles.summary_en: The review analyzes field-dependent conductivity materials that can autonomously grade electric fields, reduce local stress, and limit leakage in high-power electrical and electronic systems. It surveys conduction mechanisms, material-tailoring strategies, applications, and remaining engineering challenges.

articles.title_original: Synergistic Interfacial Engineering in V2C MXene Heterostructures for Enhanced Nano-aluminum Reactivity
articles.title_en: V2C MXene Heterostructures Boost Nano-Aluminum Reactivity
articles.excerpt_original: Nano-aluminum (nano-Al) is a high-energy-density material with exceptional reactivity, making it promising for aerospace and military applications. Reducing particle size increases the active surface area and interfacial mass diffusion, but intrinsic agglomeration and dense alumina shells hinder diffusion. Conventional additives often reduce reactivity. Here, we modulate nano-Al interfacial diffusion through synergistic interactions in a V2C MXene heterostructure. The self-assembly of nano-Al on MXene suppresses agglomeration, while fluorine-containing terminations etch the alumina shells. The heterostructure also forms metal oxide contact layers that promote solid-phase thermite reactions. These effects increase the peak heat flow in air to 107.6 W g-1, 3.5 times that of pristine nano-Al. Solid-phase reactions complete energy release before Al melting, minimizing energy loss. The composite shows larger flame areas and a lower minimum ignition concentration (≥5 wt %). Adjusting the heating temperature reduces the total combustion duration by 88.9% and increases the dynamic pressure. This versatile fabrication process enables tunable performance for diverse operational environments.
articles.summary_en: Researchers engineered V2C MXene–nano-aluminum heterostructures that suppress agglomeration and etch alumina shells, increasing peak heat flow to 107.6 W g−1. articles.title_en: Delaminated MXene Improves Magnesium Hydride Hydrogen Release
articles.excerpt_original: Magnesium hydride (MgH2) is a promising hydrogen storage material due to its high hydrogen capacity. However, pure MgH2 demonstrates high dehydrogenation temperature and slow reaction kinetics. To overcome these limitations, in this study, delaminated Ti3C2Tx MXene was incorporated into MgH2 using a simple wet mixing process in order to improve dehydrogenation performance. It was found that increasing the MXene content from 1 to 6 wt.% decreased the onset dehydrogenation temperature of the MgH2-Ti3C2Tx composite from 242 to 218 °C, which is significantly lower than that for pure MgH2 (325 °C). The activation energy for hydrogen desorption decreased from 145 kJ/mol for materials containing 1 wt.% Ti3C2Tx to 67–70 kJ/mol for materials containing 3 or 6 wt.%, which is lower than the values reported for ball-milled MXene-MgH2 composites. The wet mixing process preserves the layered structure of MXene and offers a potentially scalable approach for industrial hydrogen storage applications.
articles.summary_en: Researchers incorporated delaminated Ti3C2Tx MXene into MgH2 via wet mixing, lowering the onset dehydrogenation temperature from 325°C for pure MgH2 to 218°C at 6 wt.% MXene. articles.title_original: From Growth to Integration: MOCVD epitaxy of h-BN and Heterogeneous Integration
articles.title_en: Review outlines MOCVD growth and integration of h-BN with graphene
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Hexagonal boron nitride (h-BN), as a two-dimensional (2D) material with outstanding structural, electrical, thermal, and optical properties, has attracted widespread attention. This review firstly summarizes the atomic structure and fundamental properties of h-BN, and provides a detailed discussion on its optical, electrical, thermal, and mechanical properties. Particularly, recent spectroscopic breakthroughs are highlighted, confirming the indirect bandgap nature of atomically thin h-BN. Subsequently, this article focuses on the process of synthesizing h-BN using metal-organic chemical vapor deposition (MOCVD), with an in-depth exploration of key parameters such as precursor control, substrate selection, temperature, and V/III ratio, and how these influence the growth process from the gas phase to nucleation. The review also addresses the strategies for thin film quality control, including epitaxial growth model, thermal annealing, and so on. Moreover, doping techniques are also discussed, covering p-type and n-type doping as well as carbon doping, to modulate the electronic properties of h-BN. Finally, he integration of h-BN into 2D and threedimensional (3D) heterostructures is further explored, particularly its van der Waals integration with other 2D materials such as graphene and transition metal dichalcogenides. Additionally, the potential of h-BN in 3D semiconductor integration is also investigated, showcasing its multifunctionality as a substrate, gate dielectric, encapsulation layer, and tunneling barrier in hybrid systems. These heterostructures can enhance the performance of electronic and optoelectronic devices. Finally, future challenges are addressed, paving the way for the development of next-generation optoelectronic and quantum devices.
articles.summary_en: The review examines metal-organic chemical vapor deposition of hexagonal boron nitride, covering precursor control, substrates, temperature, doping and film-quality strategies. It also assesses van der Waals integration with graphene and other 2D materials for semiconductor, optoelectronic and quantum-device architectures.

articles.title_original: Engineering quantum phases in two dimensions via vacancy-induced electronic reconstruction
articles.title_en: Atomic Vacancies Could Enable Topological Phases in 2D Semiconductors
articles.excerpt_original: Topological phases of matter are commonly understood as emerging from crystalline symmetry and intrinsic spin-orbit coupling or, less frequently, from disorder-driven electronic renormalization. In realistic materials, however, structural defects naturally combine both ingredients. Here, we propose a universal mechanism by which atomic vacancies drive a topological phase transitions in two-dimensional semiconductors through electronic reconstruction. We show that vacancies generate locally ordered dangling-bond states governed by well-defined hopping and spin-orbit interactions, while their spatial distribution and mutual coupling introduce long-range disorder. As vacancy concentration increases, the hybridization of these defect states forms an emergent electronic subspace that undergoes a topological transition. By combining large-scale density functional theory calculations with an interpretable orbital based Hamiltonian, we find that this vacancy-induced electronic reconstruction can stabilize quantum spin Hall, quantum anomalous Hall, and Weyl semimetal phases. Our results indicate vacancies not as detrimental perturbations, but as active design elements capable of transforming trivial insulators into topological quantum matter, providing realistic routes for defect-engineered topological devices. Topological phases of matter typically arise from crystalline symmetry and spin–orbit coupling, but structural defects in materials can also play a crucial role. Here, the authors demonstrate that atomic vacancies in two-dimensional semiconductors can induce topological phase transitions, suggesting vacancies as transformative elements for designing defect-engineered topological devices.
articles.summary_en: Researchers propose that increasing atomic-vacancy concentrations can reconstruct electronic states in two-dimensional semiconductors and induce quantum spin Hall, quantum anomalous Hall, and Weyl semimetal phases. The findings suggest a route to defect-engineered topological devices, although the work is theoretical and requires experimental validation.

articles.title_original: Negative-voltage-enabled energy efficient nonvolatile memories and in-memory computing based on 2D piezoelectric transistors

articles.excerpt_original: Piezoelectric FET (PeFET) is a promising non-volatile-memory (NVM) device that integrates a piezoelectric (PE)/ferroelectric (FE) capacitor with a 2D transistor. It uses the polarization of the FE capacitor for bit-storage and strain-induced bandgap change of the 2D channel during read. Previous PeFET-based NVM designs have shown immense promise in achieving high density and energy-efficiency compared to SRAM. However, a key limitation of these designs is that they must trade-off integration density to enhance energy-efficiency or augment the memory functionality with in-memory computing (IMC). In this work, we show that the unique structure of the PeFET presents an appealing opportunity to counter these limitations, thereby simultaneously achieving high density, high energy-efficiency, and IMC-compatibility. First, we highlight the key reasons for the limited energy-efficiency of the previous PeFET designs. Based on these insights, we propose two flavors of PeFET memories that utilize negative voltage (NeVo) to reduce the major energy-consuming components significantly. Compared to 6T-SRAM (prior PeFET-based NVMs), the proposed designs achieve substantial reductions in energy, lowering read energy to 0.08 × (0.03 × ) and write energy to 0.19 × (0.53 × ), respectively. We then leverage these cells to implement IMC primitives, such as addition, subtraction, and multiply-and-accumulate (MAC), achieving 0.03 × the energy consumption of prior PeFET-based designs.

articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Ti3C2Tx MXene is widely employed in energy storage because of its unique interfacial charge-storage properties. Understanding its intrinsic capacitive properties, especially the surface characteristics of a monolayer flake, is critical to optimizing device performance, but direct measurement at the monolayer level remains elusive. Here, we report, for the first time, direct experimental quantification of the intrinsic capacitance of monolayer Ti3C2Tx MXene by integrating optimized flake protection and parasitic-capacitance-shielding strategies. The quasi-static areal capacitance is 141 μF cm–2 in acidic electrolytes and 61–74 μF cm–2 in alkali-metal-ion electrolytes. Decoupling the pseudocapacitive and electric-double-layer contributions by resolving the concentration dependence reveals that pseudocapacitance accounts for ∼45% of the total in acidic electrolytes but <10% in alkali-metal-ion electrolytes. Temperature-dependent kinetics show that a lower proton-transfer activation energy facilitates the pseudocapacitive charge storage. This work quantifies how redox and double-layer mechanisms coexist on a monolayer Ti3C2Tx MXene surface and establishes a benchmark across the field.
articles.summary_en: Researchers directly quantified the intrinsic capacitance of monolayer Ti3C2Tx MXene, measuring 141 μF cm–2 in acidic electrolytes and 61–74 μF cm–2 in alkali-metal-ion electrolytes. The study also separates pseudocapacitive and electric-double-layer contributions, providing benchmarks for MXene-based energy-storage design.

articles.title_original: Gill‐Inspired Biomimetic Engineering Enables 100 000‐Cycle Stable Potassium Storage of MXene
articles.title_en: Biomimetic MXene Electrode Achieves 100,000-Cycle Potassium Storage Stability
articles.excerpt_original: ABSTRACT MXene materials suffer from critical challenges including poor air stability, sheet restacking, sluggish K storage kinetics, and structural collapse during cycling. Inspired by biological interface functions, this work constructs an organic‐inorganic biomimetic MXene‐4‐MVA composite through chemical coupling between 4‐methylvaleric acid (4‐MVA) and the functionalized MXene surface. The 4‐MVA functions as a molecular pillar to expand interlayer spacing, expose active sites, and buffer volume deformation while forming a protective layer that inhibits MXene oxidation. Simultaneously, the interfacial charge redistribution induced by 4‐MVA modification generates an interfacial dipole effect, which regulates charge transfer behavior and K + adsorption kinetics. Experimental tests and density functional theory (DFT) calculations reveal that the organic modification regulates interfacial K adsorption behavior and ion transport characteristics. Consequently, the obtained MXene‐4‐MVA exhibits an excellent specific capacitance of 59.0 F g −1 at 0.5 A g −1 . The assembled aqueous symmetric MXene‐4‐MVA // MXene‐4‐MVA supercapacitor achieves an ultrahigh capacitance retention of 92.1% after 100 000 cycles at 5 A g −1 , exceeding the cycling stability of most state‐of‐the‐art supercapacitors. This study providing new insights for the design and preparation of highly stable MXene‐based energy storage electrodes.
articles.summary_en: Researchers modified MXene with 4-methylvaleric acid to expand interlayer spacing, limit oxidation, and improve potassium-ion transport. The resulting aqueous symmetric supercapacitor retained 92.1% of its capacitance after 100,000 cycles, highlighting a potentially important route to more durable MXene-based energy-storage electrodes.

articles.title_original: Engineering MXene-, LDH-, and MOF-Based NO2 Sensors for Sustainable Environmental Monitoring: Mechanisms, Performance, and Practical Challenges
articles.title_en: Review Assesses MXene, LDH and MOF Materials for NO₂ Sensors
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Nitrogen dioxide (NO2) is one of the hazardous air pollutants, and its sensitive detection requires sensors that combine low-temperature operation with high selectivity, recovery, humidity tolerance, and long-term stability. This review critically evaluates MXene-, layered double hydroxide (LDH)-, and metal–organic framework (MOF)-based materials for NO2 sensing applications. The effects of composition, morphology, porosity, defects, heterointerfaces, and conductivity are also correlated to sensing performance. MXenes provide conductive, termination-rich surfaces but are vulnerable to oxidation, restacking, humidity-dependent behavior, and incomplete recovery. On the other hand, LDHs provide compositionally tunable layered and porous structures; however, their limited conductivity necessitates the use of conductive supports or coupling with semiconductors. In contrast, MOFs and MOF-derived materials provide accessible pores, metal sites, and structurally controllable derivatives, but electrical and moisture stability remains material-dependent. Improved sensing performance is generally linked to oxygen vacancies, charge transfer, stronger adsorption, and heterojunction effects; however, these mechanisms are proposed rather than directly confirmed under actual sensing conditions. The review also discusses humidity control, theory–experiment alignment, and requirements for wireless deployment. Practical use may require standardized testing, long-term stability assessment, full device power analysis, and validation under realistic conditions.
articles.summary_en: An academic review compares MXene-, layered double hydroxide- and metal–organic framework-based materials for low-temperature NO₂ sensing, highlighting trade-offs in conductivity, humidity tolerance, recovery and stability. It identifies standardized testing, long-term validation and realistic deployment conditions as priorities for practical environmental monitoring.

articles.title_original: Carbon Fiber Reinforced Polymer Composites Using Nanoscale MXene-CNT Interfacial Engineering for Mechanical and Electromagnetic Shielding
articles.title_en: MXene–CNT Interface Engineering Boosts Carbon-Fiber Composite Strength and EMI Shielding
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Surface modification of carbon fibers (CFs) is critical for achieving high-performance and multifunctional CF-reinforced composites. In this work, a synergistic interfacial engineering strategy was developed by co-grafting aminated MXenes and carbon nanotubes (CNTs) onto CF surfaces after nitric acid oxidation. The successful co-grafting of nanomaterials with different dimensionalities constructed a robust and multifunctional interfacial layer, whose effects on wettability, tensile strength, electrical conductivity, Interlaminar shear strength (ILSS), mechanical properties, and electromagnetic interference (EMI) shielding performance of composites were systematically investigated. FTIR and XPS confirmed the introduction of abundant polar functional groups and a roughened surface morphology, resulting in improved interfacial wettability and adhesion with the epoxy matrix. Benefiting from the synergistic interfacial modification, the CF-MXenes/CNTs@epoxy composites exhibited increases in mechanical performance, with ILSS and flexural strength increasing by 32.57% and 125.5%, respectively, compared with unmodified CF composites. Meanwhile, the interconnected conductive network formed at the modified fiber−matrix interface endowed the composites with excellent EMI shielding capability, achieving a total shielding effectiveness of 38.21 dB in the X-band, dominated by absorption. The simultaneous improvement in mechanical properties and EMI shielding performance originates from the synergistic effects of chemical bonding, mechanical interlocking, conductive network construction, and interfacial polarization.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a nanoscale MXene–carbon nanotube interfacial treatment for carbon-fiber/epoxy composites, increasing interlaminar shear strength by 32.57% and flexural strength by 125.5% versus unmodified composites. The modified materials achieved 38.21 dB electromagnetic-interference shielding in the X-band, indicating potential relevance for structural and shielding applications.

articles.title_original: Microfluidic Architecting of Patchy MXene Core‐Shell Particles for Ultralow‐Loading Photothermal Shape‐Memory Actuation
articles.title_en: Microfluidic MXene Particles Enable Ultralow-Loading Photothermal Shape-Memory Actuation
articles.excerpt_original: ABSTRACT Shape memory polymers capable of remote actuation are promising for soft robotics, adaptive structures, and biomedical devices, yet efficient photothermal actuation remains limited by particle aggregation, localized thermal hotspots, and poor energy utilization. Here, we introduce a microfluidic architecture‐engineering strategy that transforms MXene nanosheets into spatially distributed patchy core–shell particles for efficient near‐infrared (NIR)‐triggered actuation at ultralow loadings. Flow‐focusing microfluidics assembles Ti 3 C 2 T x MXene nanosheets into 7–10 nm patchy shells around polymeric cores, suppressing restacking while maximizing accessible photothermal interfaces. Incorporated into poly(L‐lactic acid), these particles enable the composite to reach its glass‐transition temperature within 10 s under NIR irradiation (850 nm, 1.8 W cm −2 ) at MXene loading of only 0.0024 wt%, resulting in ≈95% shape recovery within 25 s. In contrast, composites containing directly dispersed MXene exhibit localized heating and achieve only ≈63% recovery after 150 s. Combining Monte Carlo photon transport and finite‐element thermal simulations, we show that the patchy‐shell architecture enhances photon harvesting and volumetric heat generation by spatially distributing photothermal interfaces throughout the material. This work establishes architecture‐controlled photothermal transport as a design principle for next‐generation smart composites and demonstrates microfluidic engineering of functional particle architectures as a scalable route toward high‐performance remotely actuated materials.
articles.summary_en: Researchers engineered patchy MXene core–shell particles using microfluidics, enabling poly(L-lactic acid) composites to achieve approximately 95% shape recovery under near-infrared irradiation at only 0.0024 wt% loading. The architecture reduced aggregation and improved heat distribution compared with directly dispersed MXene, indicating potential for remotely actuated smart composites.

articles.title_original: Predictive Wear Depth Analysis of Al–GnP–hBN Hybrid Nanocomposites Through Machine Learning Techniques
articles.title_en: Machine Learning Predicts Wear in Aluminium–Graphene–hBN Composites
articles.excerpt_original: Reinforcement content and sliding duration strongly influence the wear behaviour of aluminium (Al)-based hybrid composites, and evaluating these parameters experimentally remains time-consuming and resource-challenging. This study presents an extensive machine-learning framework to forecast the wear depth of Al-graphene nanoplatelet (GnP)-hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) hybrid nanocomposites with a data set of 3,016 experimentally obtained measurements, with wt% reinforcement and sliding time as inputs. Five supervised regression models (Linear Regression, Support Vector Regression, Multi-Layer Perceptron, Random Forest and Extreme Gradient Boosting) were trained and evaluated with the performance metrics of R2, root mean square error and mean squared error. The minimal prediction error with the highest accuracy (R2 ≈ 1.000) was obtained with the Random Forest model, exceeding both linear and kernel-based approaches capable of describing the non-linear wear responses shown by Al hybrid composites. SHAP analysis indicated that sliding time is the dominant factor governing wear depth, while reinforcement wt% contributes secondary but meaningful effects. The projected machine learning-driven method delivers a fast, dependable and characterisation-free method for expecting wear behaviour and delivers interpretable insights into parameter influence, offering a valuable tool for the design and optimisation of Al hybrid nanocomposites for advanced engineering applications.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed and evaluated five machine-learning models using 3,016 experimental measurements to predict wear depth in aluminium–graphene nanoplatelet–hBN hybrid nanocomposites. Random Forest achieved the highest reported accuracy, while SHAP analysis identified sliding time as the dominant factor and reinforcement content as a secondary influence.

articles.title_original: Localization Contrast As a Fundamental Limit of Radiative Quantum Efficiency
articles.title_en: Localization Contrast Limits Radiative Quantum Efficiency in InGaN
articles.excerpt_original: Disorder can localize valence- and conduction-band states to different degrees, yet whether such localization contrast has observable consequences remains poorly understood. Here, we show that localization contrast strongly impacts competing carrier-recombination channels. We illustrate this behavior in random In$_x$Ga$_{1-x}$N alloys. Increasing the In content from $x=13.5\%$ to $x=22\%$ progressively localizes the valence-band maximum state while leaving the conduction-band minimum state comparatively delocalized. This contrasting localization decreases the interband optical momentum matrix element underlying radiative recombination. For Auger-Meitner recombination, however, localization alone does not determine the coupling; atomic-scale disorder also breaks primitive-cell translational symmetry and modifies the momentum-space and phase structure of the states. This generates additional low-$Q$ components and enhances the Auger coupling by more than five orders of magnitude relative to pristine GaN. Thus, we provide a microscopic explanation for the competing trends in radiative and Auger recombination. More broadly, our results establish localization contrast as a mechanism through which disorder can control optical and carrier-carrier interactions in semiconductors.
articles.summary_en: A study finds that differing localization of valence- and conduction-band states in disordered InGaN reduces radiative recombination while substantially enhancing Auger–Meitner coupling. The results identify localization contrast and atomic-scale disorder as mechanisms controlling competing carrier-recombination pathways in semiconductors.

articles.title_original: Strain-tunable ZrS$$_2$$-1 H/ZrS$$_2$$-1T van der Waals heterostructures with quasi Type-II band alignment for solar oxygen evolution and optoelectronic applications
articles.title_en: Strain-Tunable ZrS₂ H/1T Van der Waals Heterostructures for Solar and Optoelectronic Applications
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract We report a first-principles study of ZrS $$_2$$ 2 -1 H and ZrS $$_2$$ 2 -1T monolayers, and their compositionally identical ZrS $$_2$$ 2 -1 H/ZrS $$_2$$ 2 -1T van der Waals heterostructure. This platform allows phase, stacking, and strain effects to be isolated without altering composition. The 1 H and 1T monolayers display HSE06 bandgaps of 1.32 and 2.16 eV. Orbital analysis shows quasi type-II band alignment, with the CBM from Zr- d states of 1 H and VBM from S- p states of 1T, facilitating charge separation.
