Calculated electron and hole effective masses are 1.03 $$m_0$$ m 0 and 0.26 $$m_0$$ m 0 , with mobilities of 9.1 and 120 cm $$^2$$ 2 V $$^{-1}$$ - 1 s $$^{-1}$$ - 1 , respectively. The heterostructure exhibits strong, tunable optical absorption from visible to UV, peaking at 0.65 $$\times $$ × 10 $$^6$$ 6 cm $$^{-1}$$ - 1 near 4.3 eV for 1T. These findings indicate that ZrS $$_2$$ 2 -1 H/ZrS
articles.summary_en: First-principles calculations indicate that compositionally identical ZrS₂ 1H/1T heterostructures exhibit quasi-Type-II band alignment, enabling charge separation. Strain tuning preserves semiconducting behavior while modifying band edges, carrier properties, and visible-to-UV optical absorption, suggesting potential for solar oxygen evolution and optoelectronics.

articles.title_original: Datapath Width Design Space of 32-Bit RISC-V Processors for 2D Semiconductor Logic
articles.title_en: Datapath Design Trade-offs for 32-Bit RISC-V Processors on 2D Semiconductors
articles.excerpt_original: The first 32-bit RISC-V processor on a two-dimensional semiconductor, a 5,931-transistor MoS2 chip, is bit-serial to fit a device-count-limited process. This work determines where the optimal datapath width departs from bit-serial execution. A digit-serial RV32I core of 1 to 32 bits is synthesized onto a model of that process, with every mapping and pipelining step formally proved. Serialization saves only about 2.5× in transistors, not 32×, because control and state do not scale with width. At the fabricated 1 kHz clock a 32-bit core thus delivers 13.5× the throughput at 5.2-5.5× lower energy per instruction. The energy ordering reverses when the throughput is fixed and the core cannot be power-gated. At the 2025 device parameters only yield selects bit-serial execution, above about 250 defects per million transistors if the 17-stage depth rule of the process is a delay budget, or 75 if it is a hard constraint. Mapper quality moves these values by up to 2.3×. Under the Poisson statistics every design yields below 1% at the published defect density, and a 10% die yield requires a 3.6-5.4× lower density, less with defect clustering. With an on-die register file, serialization saves only 11-13% of the transistors, and bit-serial execution is never the widest feasible design. Closed-form boundaries locate other technologies on this width map.
articles.summary_en: Researchers analyze datapath widths for RISC-V processors implemented on MoS2-based 2D semiconductor logic. The study finds that wider designs can substantially improve throughput and energy efficiency, while fabrication yield and defect density limit practical architectures.

articles.title_original: Predicting excess solvation in binary solvents toward green organic semiconductor processing
articles.title_en: ShellEx Model Predicts Green Solvent Mixtures for Organic Semiconductor Inks
articles.excerpt_original: Replacing halogenated solvents in organic semiconductor inks benefits from binary mixtures that balance dissolution and film drying, yet mixing changes solvation beyond the pure-solvent contributions. Here, we introduce ShellEx, a three-dimensional contact-shell model distilled from openCOSMO-RS that predicts this endpoint-fixed excess solvation from force-field geometries. Trained on 10,640 calculated curves for aromatic cores resembling organic semiconductors, ShellEx reduces the error by 27% on held-out curves relative to a zero-excess reference, which interpolates linearly between pure-solvent free energies. On 148 measured curves of eight solutes, its error, averaged with equal weight per solute, is similar to that of openCOSMO-RS and below that of simpler baselines. An openCOSMO-RS map of 200 solvent pairs for 35 cores ranks limonene–γ-valerolactone first among six predefined candidate-green pairs, with a median 1.35-fold concentration gain over the zero-excess reference. ShellEx selects the same pair and reproduces the pair ranking with a Spearman correlation of 0.85. ShellEx thus offers a route to prioritize green binary solvent pairs and compositions for halogen-free organic semiconductor inks before experimental testing.
articles.summary_en: Researchers introduced ShellEx, a contact-shell model that predicts excess solvation in binary solvents and reduces error by 27% versus a zero-excess reference on held-out data. It identified limonene–γ-valerolactone as the top candidate among evaluated green solvent pairs, supporting halogen-free ink formulation before experimental testing.

articles.title_original: Semiconductor d‐Band Engineering for Enhanced Photocatalytic Nitrogen Fixation: Progress and Perspectives
articles.title_en: Review Examines d-Band Engineering for Photocatalytic Nitrogen Fixation
articles.excerpt_original: ABSTRACT Regulating the d‐band center of semiconductors through elemental doping presents a promising strategy for enhancing the efficiency of photocatalytic nitrogen conversion. This review systematically summarizes recent advances in d‐band center engineering for photocatalytic nitrogen fixation. It begins with a concise introduction to the fundamental principles and mechanisms of photocatalytic nitrogen fixation. The core d‐band center theory is subsequently elaborated, detailing how the position of the d‐band center governs catalytic activity. In discussing its applications, the review examines the influence of metal surface configurations and electric field modulation on the electronic structure, emphasizing how precise heteroatom doping can effectively tune the d‐band center. To further improve photocatalytic nitrogen fixation performance, targeted strategies for d‐band center regulation are proposed. These include: (i) modulating adsorption energies via elemental doping, and precisely controlling the number of d‐electrons through valence state adjustment, redox tuning, or charge transfer induction and (ii) adjusting the d‐band width, thereby influencing the d‐band center position and adsorption energy, through the introduction of tensile/compressive strain or by altering the coordination number and strength. Finally, this review concludes with a perspective on the implications of d‐band center engineering for photocatalytic nitrogen fixation, aiming to provide a comprehensive understanding of both the theoretical framework and its practical applications in this field.
articles.summary_en: The review surveys how elemental doping, valence-state tuning, charge transfer, strain, and coordination changes can regulate semiconductor d-band centers and improve photocatalytic nitrogen conversion. It outlines strategies for controlling adsorption energies and electronic structure while identifying directions for future research.

articles.title_original: Modeling the Temperature and Magnetic Field Dependence of the Band Gap in Narrow-Zone Quantum Well Semiconductors
articles.title_en: Modeling Band-Gap Dependence in Narrow-Zone Quantum Wells
articles.excerpt_original: The fundamental physical parameter of both bulk and low-dimensional semiconductor structures is the band gap (𝐸𝑔 3𝑑 ,𝐸𝑔 2𝑑 ), whose energetic width allows the prediction of the operational parameters of semiconductor-based devices in advance. Therefore, the determination of 𝐸𝑔 3𝑑 and 𝐸𝑔 2𝑑 (in cases where the band gap of newly synthesized materials is not known) is considered one of the primary tasks in semiconductor heterostructure technology. Furthermore, another important feature of 𝐸𝑔 is its strong sensitivity to external influences. Indeed, variations in 𝐸𝑔 resulting from such effects can fundamentally alter the physical and chemical properties of semiconductor devices.
articles.summary_en: The study models how temperature and magnetic fields affect the band gap of narrow-zone quantum-well semiconductors. Such modeling can support prediction of operating parameters in semiconductor heterostructures and devices.

articles.title_original: On‐Surface Non‐Equilibrium Phase Evolution Toward 2D Supramolecular Glass
articles.title_en: Non-Equilibrium 2D Supramolecular Glass Formed on Silver
articles.excerpt_original: Controlling crystalline-to-glassy transitions represents a vibrant frontier in supramolecular chemistry and condensed matter physics, providing fundamental insights into non-equilibrium dynamics and enabling functional tunability for elasticity electronics and phase-change devices. Conventional two-dimensional (2D) supramolecular assembly follows an enthalpy-dominated thermodynamic paradigm, restricting the exploration of non-equilibrium supramolecular glasses (SMGs). Herein, we report the controlled construction of a non-equilibrium SMG on Ag(111) using in situ-generated triradical triphenyl-triazine molecules. The electrophilic triazine core enriches charge density at radical sites and strengthens molecule-substrate interfacial coupling, imposing pronounced kinetic constraints at the surface. Upon thermal activation, the system follows a non-monotonic, four-phase evolution that involves a thermodynamically uphill transformation. Rather than directly relaxing to the global thermodynamic minimum, it is kinetically arrested into a metastable glassy state with short-range order and long-range disorder. This work revises the conventional enthalpy-dominated view of supramolecular assembly and establishes a backbone-modulated radical kinetic strategy for rational fabrication of disorder-tunable 2D supramolecular materials.
articles.summary_en: Researchers constructed a metastable two-dimensional supramolecular glass on Ag(111) using triradical triphenyl-triazine molecules. The observed four-phase, kinetically constrained evolution could support tunable disorder in future electronic and phase-change materials.

articles.title_original: Turning graphene into an intensity gauge for Angle-Resolved Photoemission Spectroscopy
articles.title_en: Graphene Enables Quantitative ARPES Intensity Calibration
articles.excerpt_original: Angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) provides the most direct experimental access to electronic band structures and many-body interactions in solids. Beyond energy and momentum, the measured intensity also carries detailed information about the initial-state wavefunction through the complex photoemission matrix element governing the transition to—and scattering character of—the photoelectron final state. Orbital tomography seeks to exploit this sensitivity to reconstruct electronic wavefunctions. However, its quantitative implementation has been hindered by the lack of direct information on the phase of the matrix element and by the nontrivial role of solid-state scattering. Here, we overcome these limitations by achieving an experimental reconstruction of the complex photoemission matrix element in quasi-freestanding monolayer graphene (QFMLG), including both amplitude and phase. By combining circular-dichroism ARPES with linearly polarized measurements within a controlled scattered-wave framework, we determine the full matrix element over a broad kinetic-energy range. The reconstructed amplitudes exhibit pronounced channel-selective resonances and Cooper minima, directly revealing substantial solid-state modifications beyond commonly used simplified models. Leveraging this quantitative reconstruction, we establish QFMLG as an easily available intensity reference for ARPES. Its known complex matrix element enables direct normalization for the product of photon flux and detector response, allowing the determination of photoemission cross sections in other materials under identical experimental geometries. This advances orbital tomography by ARPES to a quantitatively normalized approach that separates the initial-state wavefunction from final-state scatterin
articles.summary_en: Researchers reconstructed the amplitude and phase of graphene’s complex photoemission matrix element using polarization-dependent ARPES. The result establishes quasi-freestanding monolayer graphene as an intensity reference for normalizing photon flux and detector response, supporting more quantitative orbital tomography.

articles.title_original: Nanoporous Graphene Homojunction Mediated by Interface Charge Transfer
articles.title_en: Nanoporous graphene homojunctions achieve controllable type-II band alignment
articles.excerpt_original: The construction of carbon-based hetero- or homojunctions is a key strategy for expanding their functional boundaries and enabling new quantum devices. On-surface synthesis provides a promising route for the precise fabrication of such structures. Although significant progress has been achieved in one-dimensional graphene nanoribbon hetero- or homojunctions, analogous two-dimensional systems remain largely unexplored. Here, we developed an AgTe monolayer intercalation method to fabricate nanoporous graphene (NPG) homojunctions. By controlling tellurium deposition, NPG islands spanning both the Ag(111) substrate and the AgTe monolayer were successfully synthesized. Owing to the interfacial charge transfer differences, the NPG exhibits different semiconductor behaviors on Ag(111) and the AgTe monolayer, resulting in the formation of an NPG homojunction with the type-II band alignment. The entire fabrication process of the NPG homojunctions was examined by scanning tunneling microscopy, and evidence for the type-II band alignment was obtained by scanning tunneling spectroscopy and density functional theory calculations. This intercalation strategy circumvents the randomness inherent in the synthesis of carbon-based heterostructures and offers a promising route toward two-dimensional carbon-based junctions with controllable band alignment.
articles.summary_en: Researchers fabricated nanoporous graphene homojunctions across Ag(111) and an AgTe monolayer using controlled tellurium intercalation. Interface charge-transfer differences produced distinct semiconductor behavior and type-II band alignment, suggesting a route to tunable two-dimensional carbon junctions for quantum devices.

articles.title_original: A Self‐Cleaning Solar Evaporator Based on MXene/Aramid Nanofiber Aerogels for Efficient Water Desalination
articles.title_en: MXene/Aramid Aerogel Enables Self-Cleaning Solar Desalination
articles.excerpt_original: ABSTRACT Due to its high energy conversion efficiency and broad accessibility to solar energy, interfacial solar steam generation presents a promising, and cost‐effective solution for desalination of saline water. However, salt accumulation on evaporator surfaces remains a major challenge, especially in the case of high‐salinity environments as the blockage it creates significantly hinders the efficiency as well as continuity of the evaporation process. Salt accumulation also significantly degrades the evaporator's surface over time, reducing its performance and efficiency. Researchers have explored various strategies, including surface modifications, hierarchical structural designs, and anti‐scaling coatings on evaporators. Despite promising results, achieving an optimal balance between maximum evaporation rates and energy efficiency remains a complex and ongoing challenge in this field of research. This study introduces tailor‐designed cylindrical MXene/aramid nanofiber aerogels as self‐cleaning solar evaporators that tolerate high salinity conditions and achieve evaporation rates of up to ∼2.26 kg m −2 h −1 at ∼80% efficiency. This self‐rotating photothermal evaporator exhibits periodic self‐regeneration rotation triggered by accumulated salt crystals to maintain its efficiency and performance. These findings represent a substantial advancement in solar thermal desalination technology for real‐world applications and provide a sustainable solution for efficient water purification, particularly in high‐salinity environments.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed cylindrical MXene/aramid nanofiber aerogels that self-rotate to shed accumulated salt during solar steam generation. The evaporators reportedly achieved evaporation rates of approximately 2.26 kg m−2 h−1 at about 80% efficiency under high-salinity conditions, supporting water purification applications.

articles.title_original: Displacement-Field-Induced Ionization of Defect States in High-Quality hBN
articles.title_en: Displacement Fields Ionize Defects in hBN-Encapsulated Graphene
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Encapsulation of two-dimensional (2D) materials with hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) is widely used to fabricate ultraclean van der Waals (vdW) heterostructures for optoelectronic and quantum transport studies. These devices are often operated under strong out-of-plane displacement fields that tune the electronic properties of the active 2D material, while the surrounding hBN is typically assumed to remain electronically inert. This assumption, however, neglects defect states that are present even in high-quality hBN crystals. Here, we probe their response to the applied displacement field using monolayer graphene encapsulated between hBN crystals as a sensitive charge sensor. Increasing the displacement field induces notable charge transfer between graphene and hBN, producing additional electron doping of ≈10–20 × 109 cm–2 even at the moderate displacement field (∼0.5 V nm–1), while simultaneously increasing carrier-density inhomogeneity of the graphene layer. Both effects are consistent with ionization of defect states within the hBN bandgap, with the bulk density ∼1–7 × 10–5 nm–3 varying across different hBN crystals. Our results show that displacement-field-induced defect ionization in hBN can modify the electronic response of vdW heterostructures, with direct implications for device design and interpretation of experiments.
articles.summary_en: Researchers show that moderate out-of-plane displacement fields ionize defect states in hBN, causing additional electron doping and increased carrier-density inhomogeneity in encapsulated graphene. The findings have implications for the design and interpretation of van der Waals semiconductor and quantum-transport devices.

articles.title_original: Helium-ion beam pattern imaging using irradiation-induced VB− centers in h-BN composite films
articles.title_en: h-BN Composite Films Enable Helium-Ion Beam Pattern Imaging
articles.excerpt_original: Spatially resolved characterization of helium-ion irradiation is important for beam profiling, irradiation-process control, and radiation-effects research. In this work, irradiation-induced color centers in hexagonal boron nitride (h-BN) were investigated for helium-ion beam-pattern imaging. Spherical h-BN/cycloolefin copolymer (Sh-BN/COC) composite films were irradiated with 50 keV He+ ions, while h-BN crystalline particles irradiated with 1.5 MeV Xe+ ions were examined as a comparative high-damage system. The irradiation fluence ranged from 1×1013 to 1 × 1016 ions cm−2. Following irradiation, a broad near-infrared photoluminescence (PL) band centered at approximately 820 nm was observed under 532 nm laser excitation. Room-temperature optically detected magnetic resonance features distributed around 3.45 GHz further supported the attribution of this emission to negatively charged boron-vacancy (VB−) centers. The PL intensity exhibited a non-monotonic dependence on irradiation fluence, while severe structural disorder and PL quenching occurred at the highest fluence. For beam-pattern imaging, the Sh-BN/COC composite film was irradiated through a five-slit mask and subsequently characterized by two-dimensional PL mapping. The reconstructed PL image reproduced the mask-defined irradiation pattern and resolved adjacent features separated by 40 μm. Using the conventional half-pitch definition, this feature size corresponds to a nominal equivalent spatial frequency of 12.5 line pairs per millimeter (lp/mm). These results demonstrate the feasibility of using irradiation-induced VB− centers in h-BN composite films as passive spatial recorders for post-irradiation helium-ion beam-pattern imaging.
articles.summary_en: Researchers demonstrated passive helium-ion beam imaging using irradiation-induced negatively charged boron-vacancy centers in h-BN/cycloolefin copolymer composite films. Photoluminescence mapping reproduced masked beam patterns and resolved adjacent features 40 μm apart, indicating potential for beam profiling and irradiation-process control.

articles.title_original: Toughening of Carbon Nanotube Fibers by Graphene Oxide Infiltration and Thermal Reduction: A Comparative Study of Graphene Oxide and Reduced Graphene Oxide
articles.title_en: Graphene Oxide Toughens Carbon Nanotube Fibers
articles.excerpt_original: We report a facile approach to improve the toughness of carbon nanotube (CNT) fibers through the incorporation of graphene oxide (GO) or reduced graphene oxide (rGO). CNT aerogel yarns were soaked in aqueous GO dispersions (0.18 wt%, 10 min) followed by twisting and densification with ethanol to produce CNT/GO fibers. Subsequent thermal reduction (250 °C, 24 h, −60 mm Hg) produced CNT/rGO fibers. Tensile testing (N ≥ 8), using two-tailed Welch’s t-tests, revealed significantly enhanced toughness for both hybrid CNT/GO fibers (d = 45 ± 10 µm) and CNT/rGO fibers (d = 63 ± 28 µm) compared to the neat CNT fibers (d = 37 ± 8 µm), but through distinct mechanical responses. CNT/GO fibers exhibited a significantly increased elongation from 11.7 ± 6.6 to 22.6 ± 8.4%, while maintaining comparable strength and modulus. Consequently, their toughness increased by 141% from 12.0 ± 5.2 to 28.9 ± 10.7 MJ/m3. In contrast, CNT/rGO fibers exhibited a significant increase in tensile strength from 214 ± 109 to 407 ± 171 MPa, while maintaining comparable elongation and modulus, resulting in a toughness of 19.4 ± 5.7 MJ/m3. Fracture morphology demonstrated that neat CNT fibers showed little evidence of necking, while CNT/GO and CNT/rGO hybrid fibers exhibited necking. These findings demonstrate that simple incorporation of GO or rGO into CNT fibers can significantly enhance their toughness by elongation-driven or strength-driven means, highlighting the potential to tune CNT fiber properties with graphene-based additives.
articles.summary_en: Researchers improved CNT fiber toughness by infiltrating fibers with graphene oxide or reduced graphene oxide. Graphene oxide primarily increased elongation and toughness, while reduced graphene oxide increased tensile strength, demonstrating distinct routes for tuning hybrid fiber mechanics.

articles.title_original: Growth Kinetics of Gallium Selenide on Graphene: Bridging Atomistic and Mesoscale Processes
articles.title_en: Modeling Gallium Selenide Growth on Graphene
articles.excerpt_original: Achieving uniform, wafer-scale thin layers and heterostructures remains a major challenge in the synthesis of two-dimensional (2D) semiconductors, which requires precise control of growth parameters and atomic-level insight into surface interactions. We combine density functional theory (DFT) and kinetic Monte Carlo (KMC) simulations to investigate the early stages of 2D gallium selenide (GaSe) growth on graphene and determine how GaSe domain morphology, growth rate, and nucleation density depend on the atomic fluxes and substrate temperature. The presence of Ga on the substrate is key to promoting GaSe nucleation, while a sufficiently high Se flux is required to enable 2D GaSe growth and suppress accumulation of Ga clusters. The DFT-informed KMC simulations also reveal a trade-off between the growth rate and morphology, showing that increasing the flux of Ga relative to Se promotes faster growth of GaSe and increases the surface roughness. In contrast, high substrate temperatures promote edge healing and favor the formation of compact triangular domains. These results identify a narrow window of experimental conditions for 2D GaSe growth on graphene.
articles.summary_en: Researchers used density functional theory and kinetic Monte Carlo simulations to examine how atomic fluxes and substrate temperature affect GaSe nucleation, morphology, and growth on graphene. The study identifies a narrow process window for compact, uniform 2D GaSe domains, supporting graphene-based semiconductor heterostructure development.

articles.title_original: Strain-induced structural transformations in hexagonal monolayer boron nitride. A density functional study
articles.title_en: Strain-Induced Phase Transformations Predicted in Monolayer Boron Nitride
articles.excerpt_original: In this work we theoretically study the structural transformations occurring in monolayer hexagonal boron nitride (h-BN) subjected to strong deformations. The first-principle computer simulations are based on the density functional theory employing the pseudopotentials with the exchange-correlation energy given in Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof form. Depending on the direction and the type of the strain, the simulations reveal different types of structural transformations in two-dimensional (2D) h-BN associated with the elastic failure. It is found that, under certain shear strains, there can form an ordered 2D orthorhombic phase with the 2D layer space symmetry pmmm. Thermal stability of the latter up to ~900 K is demonstrated by first-principle Born-Oppenheimer molecular dynamics. The examination of electronic structure indicates that, in contrast to the conventional h-BN, which is an insulator with the wide band gap, the predicted orthorhombic phase is expected to be a semiconductor with the narrow band gap of ~ 0.65 eV.
articles.summary_en: Density functional simulations predict that strong shear strain can transform hexagonal monolayer boron nitride into an ordered orthorhombic phase. The proposed phase remains thermally stable up to approximately 900 K and has a predicted narrow band gap of about 0.65 eV, unlike insulating conventional h-BN.

articles.title_original: A van der Waals photon-ratchet for enhancing spin-defect emission and quantum sensing
articles.title_en: Van der Waals photon ratchet boosts hBN spin-defect emission 45-fold
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Spin defects in two-dimensional materials are promising platforms for quantum information technologies and nanoscale sensing. The negatively charged boron vacancy ( $${\mathrm{V}}_{\mathrm{B}}^{-}$$ V B − ) in hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) is particularly attractive due to its sensitivity to temperature, magnetic fields, and pressure, but its application is limited by intrinsically weak photoluminescence (PL). Here we demonstrate a van der Waals heterostructure that enhances the PL intensity of $${\mathrm{V}}_{\mathrm{B}}^{-}$$ V B − by up to 45× at 4 Kelvin while preserving compatibility with ultrathin optoelectronic platforms. A quasi type-I band alignment at the PbI 2 –defected hBN interface facilitates efficient interlayer coupling to the defect, and strong spectral overlap supports fluorescence resonance energy transfer. Ab initio calculations indicate that this coupling enables a photon-ratcheting mechanism, in which optical absorption in PbI 2 generates a nonlinear polarization that drives $${\mathrm{V}}_{\mathrm{B}}^{-}$$ V B − excitation. This process is compatible with interlayer energy transfer while maintaining minimal electronic and spin hybridization and preserving optically detected magnetic resonance (ODMR) contrast. The heterostructure further exhibits improved sensitivity to external magnetic fields. These results establish a route for the enhancement of defect emission via interlayer optical coupling and introduce a general materials strategy for amplifying weak quantum defect signals in nanomaterials.
articles.summary_en: Researchers demonstrated a PbI₂–defected hexagonal boron nitride heterostructure that enhanced boron-vacancy photoluminescence by up to 45× at 4 K. The approach preserved optically detected magnetic resonance contrast and improved magnetic-field sensitivity, supporting quantum sensing and ultrathin optoelectronic applications.

articles.title_original: Impact of transition metal doping on the structural, optical and electrochemical performance of nanostructured lanthanum sesquioxide particles
articles.title_en: Nickel Doping Enhances Lanthanum Sesquioxide Nanostructure Performance
articles.excerpt_original: In this work, the microwave-precipitation process was successfully utilized to synthesize undoped lanthanum sesquioxide (ULSO) and Ni-doped lanthanum sesquioxide (NDLSO) nanostructured materials.Structural, optical and electrochemical properties of the synthesized ULSO and NDLSO samples were comprehensively characterized.Powder XRD analysis confirmed the formation of a hexagonal lanthanum sesquioxide (La2O3) crystal structure for all samples.Moreover, the crystallite size was gradually decreased with increasing Ni dopant concentration in comparison with the ULSO, which indicates that the Ni incorporation effectively reduced crystallite growth.The FTIR studies confirmed the existence of characteristic vibrational bands and functional groups of La2O3 in both ULSO and NDLSO samples.The optical absorption studies revealed an increase in the optical band gap with the increase of Ni concentration indicating the doping-induced modification of the electronic structure.Room-temperature PL emission (RTPLE) spectra exhibited intense blue-green emission arising from defect-related electronic states.Electrochemical investigations demonstrated that the NDLSO exhibited enhanced redox activity and improved charge-transfer behaviour compared with the ULSO, highlighting the beneficial influence of Ni doping on the multifunctional properties of La2O3 nanostructures.
articles.summary_en: Researchers synthesized nickel-doped lanthanum sesquioxide nanoparticles and found that doping reduced crystallite size and increased the optical band gap. The modified material also showed stronger defect-related emission, enhanced redox activity, and improved charge-transfer behavior compared with undoped lanthanum sesquioxide.

articles.title_original: Defect Stannite Structure and Cation Disorder in the Ternary Semiconductor ZnIn2Te4: Rietveld Refinement and Hirshfeld Surface Analysis
articles.title_en: ZnIn₂Te₄ Structure and Defect Chemistry Characterized
articles.excerpt_original: ZnIn2Te4, a defect-derived ternary semiconductor belonging to the II-III2-VI4 family, was synthesized by a controlled melt and long-term annealing method and structurally characterized by powder X-ray diffraction combined with Rietveld refinement. The diffraction data were successfully indexed in a tetragonal unit cell and refined in the non-centrosymmetric space group I-42m, confirming a defect stannitetype structure. The refined unit cell parameters are a = 6.1506(1) Å and c = 12.3124(2) Å, with c/a ≈ 2.00, consistent with partial cation disorder between Zn2+ and In3+ over the 2a and 4d tetrahedral sites, while preserving the ordered cation vacancy required by electron-counting rules. The structure consists of slightly distorted corner-sharing (Zn/In)Te4 tetrahedra forming a three-dimensional framework. Hirshfeld surface and fingerprint plot analyses reveal that In-Te (46.4%) and Zn-Te (26.5%) contacts dominate the packing, whereas Te-Te interactions (20.6%) reflect the presence of intrinsic vacancies within the anion sublattice. Void surface analysis confirms the existence of isolated low-density regions associated with the defect-derived nature of the compound. The combined crystallographic and topological analyses provide a consistent structural model that rationalizes the reported spin-glass behavior in Mn-doped analogues and the intrinsically low lattice thermal conductivity predicted for this material, reinforcing the relevance of ZnIn2Te4 as a promising thermoelectric semiconductor.
articles.summary_en: Researchers synthesized and structurally characterized the defect-stannite semiconductor ZnIn₂Te₄ using powder X-ray diffraction, Rietveld refinement and Hirshfeld analysis. The findings support intrinsic low lattice thermal conductivity and potential thermoelectric relevance, while clarifying cation disorder and vacancy-related structure.

articles.title_original: Intensity-driven Mott-like transition in a 2D Ruddlesden-Popper perovskite
articles.title_en: 2D Perovskite Shows Intensity-Driven Mott-Like Optical Transition
articles.excerpt_original: Two-dimensional Ruddlesden-Popper-type halide perovskites have emerged as promising cutting-edge nonlinear optical materials due to their strong excitonic effects and carrier-density-dependent optical responses. In this work, we investigate the nonlinear optical properties and ultrafast carrier dynamics of (BA)$_2$PbI$_4$ under infrared excitation, resonant with the two-photon energy of its excitonic transition. Using a nonlinear femtosecond Z-scan measurement with a 1030\,nm pump pulse, we observe a pronounced intensity-dependent evolution of the nonlinear absorption coefficient and the refractive index. With increasing pump intensity, a switch from saturable absorption to reverse saturable absorption emerges, suggesting an intensity-driven Mott-like transition. To elucidate the underlying carrier dynamics, intensity-dependent transient absorption spectroscopy was performed under the same excitation intensities. This reveals a long-lived charge carrier population above the estimated Mott density, reflecting a clear phase transition from an exciton-dominated regime to a dense electron-hole plasma regime. Moreover, such an intensity-driven, high, and switchable nonlinear optical response, along with a Mott-like transition under infrared pulse excitation, makes the 2D (BA)$_2$PbI$_4$ perovskites suitable for all-optical operation in the infrared regime.
articles.summary_en: Researchers observed a switch from saturable to reverse saturable absorption in a 2D Ruddlesden–Popper perovskite under infrared excitation. The switchable nonlinear response and transition to an electron–hole plasma regime indicate potential for all-optical infrared devices.

articles.title_original: Plasmonic Metal Nanostructures Foster the Catalytic Performance of 2D Dichalcogenide Nanomaterials
articles.title_en: Metal Nanostructures Enhance Catalysis in 2D Dichalcogenides
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) are novel materials with unique optical, electrical, and chemical properties. These properties are determined by a band gap in the infrared and visible regions of the electromagnetic spectrum. A growing body of evidence indicates that TMDs can perform light-driven catalysis of chemical reactions. Furthermore, the rate and yield of such catalytic reactions can be altered by hybridization of TMDs with metallic nanostructures. However, the underlying mechanisms of such catalysis remain unclear, as does the extent to which the catalytic properties of TMDs can be modified by the metallic nanostructures. In this study, we utilized tip-enhanced Raman spectroscopy (TERS), a novel imaging approach with nanometer spatial resolution, to investigate how hybridization of tungsten disulfide (WS2) two-dimensional nanostructures with gold (Au) and silver (Ag) nanostructures alters their catalytic properties. Specifically, we measured the yield of p,p′-dimercaptoazobisbenzene (DMAB) formed on the surfaces of WS2, WS2@Au, and WS2@Ag decorated with 4-nitrobenzenethiol (4-NBT). Our results show that Ag nanostructures substantially enhanced DMAB-associated Raman response on WS2, whereas the enhancement observed on WS2@Au was considerably less pronounced. These results indicate that metallic nanostructures can be used to enhance the catalytic properties of TMDs. Our findings also indicate that the enhancement effect directly depends on the nature of the metal nanostructures hybridized with TMDs.
articles.summary_en: Researchers used tip-enhanced Raman spectroscopy to show that silver nanostructures substantially enhanced catalytic activity indicators in WS₂, while gold produced a weaker effect. The findings link catalytic enhancement to the specific metal hybridized with the 2D material.

articles.title_original: Visualizing symmetry-broken Chern insulators and their quantum melting
articles.title_en: STM visualizes symmetry-broken Chern insulators in bilayer graphene
articles.excerpt_original: In the presence of a magnetic field, electronic states of moiré quantum materials develop a Hofstadter spectrum that provides a distinctive setting for studying the interplay between band topology and strong electron-electron interaction. Using scanning tunneling microscopy, we studied Hofstadter's states in bilayer graphene aligned with hexagonal boron nitride and directly visualized the formation of interaction-driven symmetry breaking Chern insulators. Our measurements revealed the formation of phases that double, triple, or quadruple the moiré unit cell at fractional filling of the Hofstadter bands as well as states with complex intra-unit cell wave functions. We visualized two distinct quantum phenomena in different Chern states, including quantum melting driven by the appearance and proliferation of topological defects and a quantum transition co-occurring with phase competition and separation.
articles.summary_en: Researchers used scanning tunneling microscopy to directly observe interaction-driven Chern insulating phases in bilayer graphene aligned with hexagonal boron nitride. The study identified moiré unit-cell multiplication, complex intra-cell wave functions, quantum melting, and phase transitions linked to topological defects and competing phases.

articles.title_original: Beyond Primary Nucleation: Molecular Basis of Peptide Crystal Secondary Nucleation at Soft Interface
articles.title_en: Molecular Basis of Peptide Crystal Secondary Nucleation on Graphite
articles.excerpt_original: ABSTRACT The formation of peptide 2D crystals with well‐organized molecular arrays by primary nucleation mechanism have provided an efficient way to incorporate biofunctions into the underlying single layer graphene and MoS 2 , leading to broad applications for biosensing, biomedicine and bioelectronics. Further realizing a high‐level architecture of peptide 3D crystals coupling with the underlying nanomaterials would expand its applications for the next‐generation bionanodevices, while facing a big challenge. A layer‐by‐layer stacking of 3D peptide assemblies through secondary nucleation (SN) mechanism at soft interface provides an available strategy while its molecular basis has been rarely explored. We utilized time‐resolved 3‐dimensional atomic force microscopy (3D‐AFM) to directly observe SN and growth mechanism of stacked peptide 3D crystals on highly oriented pyrolytic graphite (HOPG). Moreover, the formation details of peptide 3D crystals including nucleation sites, growth dynamics, molecular‐resolution nanostructures, phase transitions, and cross‐seeding growth were discovered. Such non‐traditional methodology in engineering peptide 3D crystals would bring new prospects for nanoscience and nanotechnology.
articles.summary_en: Researchers used time-resolved three-dimensional atomic force microscopy to observe secondary nucleation and stacked peptide crystal growth at a soft interface on highly oriented pyrolytic graphite. The findings could support peptide-based architectures for graphene-enabled biosensing, biomedicine, and bioelectronics.

articles.title_original: Bottom-up assembly of graphene-decorated d-MXene nanoarchitecture for enhanced antibacterial activity against Escherichia coli and Bacillus cereus
articles.title_en: Graphene–MXene Nanoarchitecture Shows Enhanced Antibacterial Activity
articles.excerpt_original: A bottom-up ultrasonication-assisted strategy was employed for the assembly of graphene-decorated d-MXene nanoarchitectures, and their antibacterial activity against Escherichia coli and Bacillus cereus was systematically investigated. The formation of the nanoarchitecture was confirmed through complementary morphological, structural, spectroscopic, and surface charge analyses. Scanning electron microscopy, elemental mapping, and high-resolution transmission electron microscopy observations revealed the uniform decoration of graphene nanosheets over layered d-MXene sheets, resulting in a structurally open architecture with suppressed nanosheet restacking. Powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD) analysis exhibited peak broadening, intensity variation, and modification of the low-angle (002) reflection, while comparative PXRD analysis with a composition-matched physical mixture further demonstrated disruption of the d-MXene stacking order following ultrasonication-assisted assembly. Raman spectroscopy exhibited the coexistence of graphene D (1339 cm −1 ) and G (1581 cm −1 ) bands together with the characteristic d-MXene vibrational mode at 153 cm −1 confirming preservation of defect-associated graphene domains within the assembled nanoarchitecture. Comparative Raman analysis further revealed systematic shifts in the characteristic graphene and d-MXene bands and a decrease in the I D / I G ratio from 1.83 for the physical mixture to 1.27 for the nanoarchitecture, supporting intimate interfacial organization. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy analysis revealed the coexistence of sp 2 C=C (284.1 eV), sp 3 C–C (284.7 eV), Ti–C (282.5 eV), and Ti–O (530.5 eV) bonding states, suggesting effective interfacial coupling and defect enriched surface regions after nanoarchitecture formation.
articles.summary_en: Researchers assembled graphene-decorated d-MXene nanosheets using ultrasonication, producing an open architecture with reduced restacking and evidence of interfacial coupling. The material was evaluated against Escherichia coli and Bacillus cereus, indicating potential relevance for antibacterial biomedical materials.

articles.title_original: Spontaneous Excitonic Mass Generation in Graphene Monolayers
articles.title_en: Study Reports Excitonic Mass Generation in Graphene Monolayers
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Coulomb interactions among graphene's massless Dirac fermions are unusually strong, making graphene a unique testbed for correlated quantum phases and interacting field theories. Among the predicted phases is an excitonic insulator, in which strong interactions drive spontaneous electron-hole pairing and condensation into a superfluid ground state. This transition has evaded experimental observation because unscreened long-range Coulomb interactions renormalize and enhance the Dirac velocity, keeping graphene in a weakly coupled semimetallic regime. Here, we overcome this constraint by decorating graphene with nanoscale metals that screen long-range interactions and suppress velocity renormalization. Scanning tunnelling spectroscopy down to 150 mK reveals a hard spectral gap (2Δ ≈ 14 meV) that emerges strictly at the Dirac point and is strongly susceptible to doping, temperature, and magnetic field --- signatures of a many-body rather than single-particle gap. The gap closes at an anomalously low critical temperature (Δ/ k B T c ≥ 100), consistent with a Berezinskii--Kosterlitz--Thouless transition, and coincides with a charge-density wave at q = K' - K that reflects intervalley excitonic pairing. Together, these results provide strong evidence for spontaneous excitonic mass generation in graphene, a correlated insulating phase long predicted but never before observed.
articles.summary_en: Researchers report a 14 meV spectral gap at graphene’s Dirac point after nanoscale-metal decoration, interpreting its doping, temperature and magnetic-field dependence as evidence of an excitonic insulating phase. The result could advance research into correlated quantum states and graphene-based electronic devices, although further independent validation is needed.

articles.title_original: Study on the Basic Properties of Graphene Nano Coolant

Six tests evaluated grinding performance, viscosity, thermal conductivity, sedimentation, specific heat, and heat-exchange performance. The results identified a different optimal Gr:GA ratio for each property. The 0%:1% ratio performed best in the grinding test, reducing friction and wear and improving cooling-system efficiency. The 0.075%:1% ratio had the lowest viscosity, which improved fluidity and reduced wear. The 0.05%:1% ratio provided the highest thermal conductivity, enhancing heat dissipation and reliability. The 0.025%:1% ratio produced the least sedimentation, maintained high thermal conductivity and stability, and achieved the best cooling performance with the lowest energy loss in the heat-exchange test. Accordingly, future vehicle tests should evaluate the 0.05%:1%, 0.075%:1%, and 0.025%:1% formulations for thermal conductivity, viscosity, and heat-exchange performance, respectively.

articles.title_original: High ambipolar mobility fluorinated MXene for ultrasensitive biosensing transistors
articles.title_en: Fluorinated MXene enables ultrasensitive biosensing transistors
articles.excerpt_original: Transition metal carbides and nitrides (MXenes) are emerging as transformative materials for bioelectronics. However, the advancement of MXene-based field-effect transistor (FET) biosensors is hindered by the lack of high-quality aqueous-stable materials and the low signal transduction efficiency intrinsic to their metallic nature. To address these issues, we report an ultrasensitive biosensing platform enabled by an in-situ fluorination strategy of MXene. By substituting unstable oxygen-containing terminations with chemically stable fluorine terminations in a mild reaction, we synthesized high-quality fluorinated MXene with the record-breaking ambipolar field-effect mobility (μ p = 10.42 cm 2 V −1 s −1 , μ n = 30.23 cm 2 V −1 s −1 ). The highly electronegative fluorinated interface suppresses interfacial electrical double-layer capacitance, boosting signal transduction efficiency. Consequently, the platform achieves the lowest limit of detection (LOD) of 0.26 fg ml −1 for Mycobacterium tuberculosis antigen MPT64 among MXene FETs up to date, accompanied by a high current response of 35.02% at LOD. Clinical validation across 126 serum samples demonstrated a diagnostic accuracy of 97.6% with a detection time of 38 s, exhibiting the high-performance and reliable biosensing in complex physiological environments.
articles.summary_en: Researchers report an in-situ fluorination strategy that improves MXene transistor mobility and signal transduction. articles.title_original: 2D Ti3C2Tx-MXene-patterned electrode enables highly sensitive humidity sensing
