articles.excerpt_original: Flexible, metal-free humidity sensors with high sensitivity, linear impedance response, and fast response/recovery times are vital for next-generation wearable electronics and environmental monitoring, whereas poor linearity limits the rapid and precise detection of humidity. Here, we report a metal-free humidity sensor that integrates lithographically patterned two-dimensional (2D) Ti 3 C 2 T x -MXene nanosheets (2DMS) interdigital electrodes (IDEs) with an engineered ultrathin network of 2D anatase TiO 2 nanosheets (2DTS) as the active humidity-responsive layer on a cyclic olefin copolymer (COC) substrate. The solution-processed 2DMS IDEs provide high electrical conductivity, mechanical robustness, and scalable patterning, while the 2DTS film forms a continuous, hydroxyl-rich, chemically robust surface network for reversible water adsorption and rapid proton-mediated transport. The resulting 2DMS@2DTS sensor exhibits highly linear and reversible impedance and capacitance modulation across a broad humidity range (6–86% RH), with low hysteresis, minimal change over 24 h, and a sensitivity of 4.41 × 10 5 Ω/%RH at 1 kHz. COMSOL-assisted finite element method (FEM) simulations reveal humidity-induced dielectric redistribution in the IDE’s electric field, while density functional theory (DFT) calculations demonstrate a reduced activation energy for proton (H⁺) migration under humid conditions. These theoretical insights are in excellent agreement with the experimentally observed fast, repeatable response and recovery characteristics, thereby providing a mechanistic understanding of the device’s high-performance humidity-sensing behavior. Owing to its all-2D-materials architecture and flexible COC substrate, the sensor enables practical applications, including real-time phys
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a flexible, metal-free humidity sensor combining patterned Ti₃C₂Tₓ MXene electrodes with anatase TiO₂ nanosheets on a cyclic olefin copolymer substrate. The device delivers linear, reversible sensing across 6–86% relative humidity with fast response and recovery, supporting wearable and environmental-monitoring applications.

articles.title_original: Layered Organic–MXene Heterostructures for High‐Capacity and Long‐Life Aqueous Sodium‐Ion Storage in Seawater‐Based Hybrid Electrolytes
articles.title_en: Organic–MXene Anode Enables Long-Life Sodium-Ion Storage Using Seawater-Based Electrolyte
articles.excerpt_original: ABSTRACT Aqueous sodium‐ion batteries (ASIBs) are attractive for large‐scale storage due to intrinsic safety and low cost. However, their practical applications are often limited by sluggish kinetics and the dependence on purified electrolytes. Here, we report a layered organic–MXene heterostructured anode by direct thermal polymerization of a conjugated naphthalene‐based polyimide (NPI) in the presence of multilayer Ti 3 C 2 T x MXene, forming a tightly coupled 2D architecture (NPI@MXene). NPI provides reversible imide‐carbonyl redox sites, while MXene facilitates electron transport and interfacial ion‐transfer kinetics, thereby reducing polarization and accelerating Na + storage. Benefiting from the reversible carbonyl conversion, enhanced pseudocapacitive behavior, and improved Na + diffusion kinetics, the optimized NPI@MXene anode delivers a specific capacity of 124.5 mAh g − 1 at 1.00 A g − 1 and shows excellent durability with 100.0% retention over 65 000 cycles at 15.0 A g − 1 . For practical operation, seawater is used to prepare a 1.00 M sodium acetate electrolyte with the most favorable interfacial kinetics among the tested seawater‐based electrolytes. The assembled NPI@MXene//Cu‐PBA full cell operated stably over the 0–1.60 V range and maintained its performance for 15 000 cycles.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed an NPI@MXene heterostructured anode for aqueous sodium-ion batteries, combining reversible organic redox sites with MXene-enhanced electron and ion transport. The device delivered 124.5 mAh g−1 and retained performance over 65,000 cycles, while a full cell using a seawater-derived electrolyte operated for 15,000 cycles.

articles.title_original: Magnetic MXenes: From Theoretical Predictions Toward Experimental Validation—Mechanisms, Characterization, and Emerging Applications
articles.title_en: Review Challenges Experimental Validation of Magnetic MXenes
articles.excerpt_original: MXenes, a rapidly expanding family of two-dimensional transition metal carbides, nitrides, and carbonitrides, have attracted considerable attention owing to their highly tunable electronic, mechanical, and chemical properties. Their magnetic behavior, governed by composition, surface terminations, defects, doping, strain, and heterostructure engineering, has positioned them as promising candidates for spintronics, magnetic sensing, microwave absorption, and quantum technologies. This review critically examines both theoretically predicted and experimentally observed magnetic phenomena in MXenes, with particular emphasis on distinguishing intrinsic lattice magnetism from magnetism induced by interfaces, surface chemistry, defects, and contamination. We systematically discuss the influence of transition-metal chemistry, surface functionalization, and external stimuli on magnetic ordering, while evaluating density functional theory predictions alongside available experimental evidence and advanced magnetic characterization techniques. Unlike previous reviews, this work focuses on the persistent gap between computational predictions and reproducible experimental observations, highlighting the limited experimental verification of intrinsic magnetic order in MXenes. Current evidence indicates that most reported magnetic responses arise from extrinsic effects rather than robust intrinsic lattice magnetism. By identifying the key factors limiting reproducibility and proposing priorities for future experimental validation, this review provides a critical framework for the rational development of magnetic MXenes and their future device applications.
articles.summary_en: This review assesses magnetic behavior in MXenes, emphasizing the gap between theoretical predictions and reproducible experimental evidence. It concludes that many reported magnetic responses likely arise from extrinsic effects such as interfaces, defects, surface chemistry, or contamination, while outlining priorities for validation and potential applications in sensing, spintronics, microwave absorption, and quantum technologies.

articles.title_original: Construction of Uniform Thermal Network in Passive Radiative Cooling Coatings by Nanocellulose-Mediated Pickering Emulsion Template
articles.title_en: Nanocellulose-templated boron nitride coatings improve radiative cooling
articles.excerpt_original: Developing high-performance passive radiative cooling coatings (PRCC) with high thermal conductivity for fast heat dissipation from self-heating objects remains a significant challenge. In this study, a nanocellulose-mediated Pickering emulsion strategy was employed to construct a uniform hexagonal boron nitride (BN) thermal network within PRCC. Benefiting from the Pickering emulsion template stabilized by TEMPO-oxidized cellulose nanofibrils (TOCNF), BN nanosheets and other functional inorganic nanoparticles were uniformly dispersed in the PRCC matrix, forming a continuous and homogeneous thermally conductive network. This structural design endowed the PRCC with excellent thermal conductivity, high solar reflectance in the solar spectrum (0.3–2.5 μm), and strong emissivity in the “atmospheric window” (ATSW, 8–13 μm). Specifically, the thermal conductivity of the TOCNF-BN-modified PRCC reached 2.28 ± 0.15 W·m−1·K−1, which was significantly higher than that of the pristine PRCC. The coating exhibited a solar reflectivity of ~87% and an emissivity of ~93% in the ATSW. Outdoor model temperature tests indicated that the internal temperature of the PRCC-TOCNF-BN-coated metal cabinet was 9.6 °C lower than that of the bare cabinet and 6.7 °C lower than the cabinet coated with pristine PRCC. This novel approach of using Pickering emulsion templates to fabricate highly thermally conductive radiative cooling coatings provides a new strategy for the development of high-performance and multifunctional radiative cooling materials for thermal management applications.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed passive radiative cooling coatings containing a uniform hexagonal boron nitride thermal network formed using nanocellulose-stabilized Pickering emulsions. The coating reached 2.28 W·m⁻¹·K⁻¹ thermal conductivity and reduced the temperature of a coated metal cabinet by 9.6 °C versus an uncoated cabinet.

articles.title_original: The Spectroscopic Atlas of Excitonic Complexes in hBN-Encapsulated S-TMD Monolayers: From Excitons to Oxcitons and Beyond
articles.title_en: Spectroscopic Atlas Maps Excitonic States in hBN-Encapsulated TMD Monolayers
articles.excerpt_original: Hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) encapsulation has transformed the optical spectroscopy of semiconducting transition-metal dichalcogenide monolayers (MLs) by suppressing extrinsic disorder and enabling the resolution of an increasingly complex hierarchy of excitonic states. This Review provides a spectroscopy-oriented framework for understanding and identifying excitonic complexes in hBN-encapsulated Mo- and W-based MLs and their alloys. The discussion covers bright and dark excitons, Rydberg states, charged excitons, biexcitons, phonon-assisted replicas, and higher-order Fermi-sea many-body states, including hexcitons and oxcitons, with an emphasis on the experimental signatures that distinguish them. Particular attention is given to the combined use of photoluminescence and absorption-related spectroscopy, electrostatic gating, polarization analysis, excitation-power and temperature dependences, magnetic fields, and time-resolved measurements to establish microscopic assignments. The role of alloying as an additional degree of freedom for engineering the excitonic hierarchy, spin-valley configuration, and magneto-optical response is also highlighted. By organizing the rapidly expanding phenomenology around experimentally accessible fingerprints rather than individual material systems, this Review aims to provide a practical and broadly applicable guide for identifying, comparing, and engineering excitonic states in high-quality two-dimensional semiconductors.
articles.summary_en: A review organizes the expanding hierarchy of excitonic complexes in hBN-encapsulated transition-metal dichalcogenide monolayers, including bright and dark excitons, Rydberg states, biexcitons, hexcitons and oxcitons. It identifies spectroscopy, gating, polarization, temperature, magnetic-field and time-resolved signatures for assigning and engineering these states in two-dimensional semiconductors.

articles.title_original: Noise-Suppressed High-Performance WSe2 Phototransistors Enabled by Optically Programmed Remote Contact Doping
articles.title_en: Remote Contact Doping Improves WSe2 Phototransistor Performance
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Improving the sensitivity of two-dimensional semiconductor phototransistors requires increasing photocurrent while minimizing noise. However, conventional doping approaches often place charged dopants in or near atomically thin channels, introducing charge scattering, trap states, and noise that limit the signal-to-noise ratio. Here, we address this signal-noise trade-off in WSe2 phototransistors by using photoinduced charge trapping in patterned hBN to implement contact-selective remote doping. Under illumination with a negative gate voltage, trapped holes in hBN electrostatically n-dope WSe2 while remaining spatially separated from the transport channel. Patterned hBN confines the doping to selected regions, allowing the WSe2 near the metal electrodes to be remotely doped while leaving the channel undoped. This remote contact doping simultaneously suppressed the device noise by approximately 100–fold, reduced the effective density of electrically active traps by approximately 100–fold, and lowered the activation energy by 30–80 meV, indicating improved contact quality and more efficient carrier injection. As a result, the contact-doped phototransistors simultaneously exhibit enhanced responsivity of 99.7 A/W and a specific detectivity of 2.26 × 1011 Jones. These results establish optically programmed remote contact doping as a phototransistor-compatible contact-engineering approach to overcome the signal–noise trade-off in 2D phototransistors.
articles.summary_en: Researchers used optically programmed charge trapping in patterned hBN to remotely dope WSe2 near metal contacts while leaving the channel undoped. The approach reportedly reduced noise and active traps by about 100-fold and achieved 99.7 A/W responsivity with a detectivity of 2.26 × 10¹¹ Jones.

articles.title_original: The Quest for the Ideal Power Transistor: Are Ultra-Wide Bandgap Devices the Answer?
articles.title_en: Ultra-Wide-Bandgap Semiconductors Could Enable Near-Ideal Power Transistors
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Power devices are undergoing a renaissance, driven by wide bandgap semiconductors such as gallium nitride and silicon carbide, which are rapidly displacing traditional silicon devices in electric vehicles, data centres, consumer electronics, and other key applications. On the horizon, a new class of ultra-wide bandgap materials—including aluminium gallium nitride alloys, diamond, and gallium oxide—is emerging. Thanks to their excellent material properties, these semiconductors could, in theory, enable near-ideal transistor performance with lower conduction and switching losses, as well as smaller chip footprints. In this perspective paper, we examine complexities associated with deep dopants, passivation layer selection, and the electro-thermal response during fast switching such as short-circuit events. We unravel root causes behind performance limitations and outline key innovations required to pave a path to market for devices based on these promising but challenging materials.
articles.summary_en: A perspective paper examines whether aluminium gallium nitride, diamond and gallium oxide can outperform silicon, gallium nitride and silicon carbide in power devices. It highlights deep dopants, passivation and electro-thermal switching challenges that must be resolved for commercial deployment.

articles.title_original: Phase-change thermal energy storage: Materials, thermophysics and emerging applications
articles.title_en: Review Examines Phase-Change Thermal Energy Storage Materials and Systems
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Phase change materials (PCMs) can reversibly store and release considerable thermal energy through nearly isothermal and isometric phase state transitions, thus have attracted broad attention in energy decarbonization, passive thermal management, and emerging fields such as medicine and intelligent robots. However, critical challenges at material, device, and system levels remain to be addressed. These include the development of pure or composite PCMs with superior thermophysical properties, the design of effective latent heat storage devices, and the optimization of system integration. This review provides a comprehensive overview of phase change thermal storage, beginning with the mechanisms underlying the regulation of PCMs’ thermophysical properties. We summarize recent advances in the physical and chemical modification of PCMs by molecular engineering, multi-component doping, and rational design of composite microstructure and morphology to improve thermodynamic and heat-transfer performance. We then highlight advanced latent heat storage device design using passive and active strategies for increasing both energy and power density, and outline PCM-integrated systems across multifunctional applications including energy harvesting and storage, thermal management, medical treatment, intelligent machine, and catalysis. Finally, we discuss future research directions towards next-generation PCMs, high-performance devices and intelligent system integration.
articles.summary_en: This review surveys advances in phase-change materials, including molecular engineering, multi-component doping, and composite microstructure design to improve thermophysical and heat-transfer performance. It also assesses latent-heat device architectures and PCM-integrated applications spanning thermal management, energy storage, medicine, and intelligent machines.

articles.title_original: Room-Temperature Multiferroicity in van der Waals Fe-Doped SnSe Semiconductors
articles.title_en: Fe-Doped SnSe Enables Room-Temperature Multiferroicity
articles.excerpt_original: Two-dimensional (2D) materials hosting multiple ferroic orders are highly desirable for next-generation electronic and spintronic technologies.However, achieving stable and tunable ferroic functionalities at room temperature remains a key challenge. Here, we report the growth of van der Waals (vdWs) Fe-doped SnSe semiconductor that can be exfoliated down to thin layered flakes. These crystals exhibit tunable ferromagnetism well above room temperature, with the Curie temperature increasing from 342 K to over 400 K through controlled Fe incorporation. In parallel, anomalous Hall measurements reveal interfacial spin polarization at the SnSe/Pt interface driven by magnetic proximity effects, enabling spin-dependent magnetotransport. Furthermore, robust ferroelectric behavior at room temperature is confirmed by piezoresponse force microscopy. Although the ferromagnetic and ferroelectric orders coexist within the same material system, they originate from distinct mechanisms without direct magnetoelectric coupling. The semiconducting nature of Fe-doped SnSe is supported by both theoretical and experimental analyses which further enhances its multifunctionality. These results establish Fe-doped SnSe as a versatile vdWs platform for integrating magnetic, electric, and electronic functionalities in future energy-efficient devices.
articles.summary_en: Researchers report exfoliatable van der Waals Fe-doped SnSe semiconductors with tunable ferromagnetism above room temperature and confirmed room-temperature ferroelectricity. The material also shows spin-polarized transport at a SnSe/Pt interface, supporting potential energy-efficient spintronic and multifunctional electronic devices.

articles.title_original: Two-Dimensional Indium Selenide for Next-Generation Photodetection: Interface Engineering, Device Architectures, and Emerging Applications
articles.title_en: Review Maps 2D Indium Selenide Photodetector Advances and Challenges
articles.excerpt_original: Two-dimensional (2D) indium selenide (InSe) has emerged as a compelling semiconductor platform for next-generation photodetection because of its thickness-tunable bandgap, high carrier mobility, and strong light-matter interaction. Moreover, its nonlinear, ferroelectric, piezoelectric, and polarization‑related functionalities can be modulated by phase, layer number, stacking configuration, and device architecture. This Review summarizes the recent advances in InSe-based photodetectors through a structure-property-performance framework. We first discuss the crystal structures, thickness-dependent band evolution, and preparation strategies of InSe and then compare representative device architectures including single-InSe channels, van der Waals heterostructures, ferroelectric-gated devices, asymmetric Schottky contacts, optical microcavities, and plasmonic/metasurface contact designs. Particular attention is paid to contact engineering, interface regulation, dark-current suppression, carrier-extraction acceleration, and polarization-selective detection, which have become central routes for improving sensitivity, speed, stability, and multifunctionality. Recent applications in optical sensing, broadband and polarization-resolved imaging, flexible and wearable electronics, neuromorphic vision, and secure optical communication are further reviewed. Finally, the remaining challenges associated with wafer-scale growth, defect control, environmental stability, standardized benchmarking, complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor (CMOS)-compatible integration, and system-level deployment are critically discussed. By emphasizing both recent progress and unresolved bottlenecks, this Review aims to provide a clearer roadmap for developing practical, high-performance InSe-based optoele
articles.summary_en: A review examines interface engineering, device architectures, and applications for indium selenide photodetectors, including optical sensing, imaging, flexible electronics, neuromorphic vision, and secure optical communication. It identifies wafer-scale growth, defect control, environmental stability, benchmarking, and CMOS integration as key barriers to deployment.

articles.title_original: Thickness‐Controlled, Centimeter‐Scale 2D Cu 2 Te Films for 2.2 µm Photodetection
articles.title_en: Centimeter-Scale 2D Cu₂Te Films Enable 2.2 µm Photodetection
articles.excerpt_original: ABSTRACT Two‐dimensional (2D) narrow‐bandgap semiconductors hold great promise in the field of mid‐infrared (MIR) optoelectronics due to their suitable bandgaps and unique physical properties. However, the controllable and scalable synthesis of 2D narrow‐bandgap semiconductors with precise thickness, stoichiometry, and lateral dimensions remains challenging. Here, the controllable synthesis of centimeter‐scale ultrathin 2D Cu 2 Te films via pulsed laser deposition (PLD) is reported, with the maximum lateral dimension of the fabricated films reaching 2 cm. The film thickness can be precisely controlled by the number of laser pulses while maintaining near‐stoichiometric composition, reaching a minimum thickness of two layers. Furthermore, photodetectors based on 2D Cu 2 Te exhibit a responsivity as high as 22 mA/W at a wavelength of 2200 nm, with a response time of approximately 15 ms, limited by the present modulation setup. This work establishes a scalable strategy for the synthesis of high‐quality 2D narrow‐bandgap material and highlights the potential of 2D Cu 2 Te for infrared optoelectronic applications.
articles.summary_en: Researchers report pulsed-laser deposition of thickness-controlled, near-stoichiometric 2D Cu₂Te films up to 2 cm laterally and as thin as two layers. Devices achieved 22 mA/W responsivity at 2.2 µm, indicating potential for scalable mid-infrared optoelectronics.

articles.title_original: Spin-valley relaxation of Rydberg excitons
articles.title_en: Rydberg excitons enable tunable spin-valley dynamics in WSe₂
articles.excerpt_original: Rydberg excitons, characterized by large spatial extension and reduced electron-hole overlap, must have a spin-valley dynamics different from that of ground state excitons. Here we report a direct measurement of spin relaxation of Rydberg excitons in high-quality WSe2 monolayer using continuous-wave and time-resolved optical orientation experiments. Excited excitonic states exhibit exceptionally large photoluminescence circular polarization, approaching 90% for the 3s state. Time-resolved measurements reveal a strong increase of the spin relaxation time with the principal quantum number, from ~2 ps for the 1s exciton to ~75 ps for the 3s exciton. A microscopic model based on electron-hole exchange-driven spin relaxation quantitatively reproduces the observed trend, demonstrating that Rydberg excitons enable tunable spin-valley dynamics in two-dimensional semiconductors.
articles.summary_en: Researchers directly measured spin relaxation in Rydberg excitons in monolayer WSe₂, finding that relaxation time increases from approximately 2 ps for the 1s state to 75 ps for the 3s state. The findings demonstrate tunable spin-valley dynamics for two-dimensional semiconductor systems.

articles.title_original: Defect-Engineered WSe2 Surface to Improve the Growth of Semimetal-Like Sn Contact
articles.title_en: Defect-Engineered WSe₂ Enables Lower-Resistance Tin Contacts
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) are promising for further device scaling. However, their practical application is hindered by high contact resistance at the metal–TMD interface. This issue originates from the van der Waals (vdW) gap, which introduces a tunneling barrier, and from metal-induced gap states (MIGS), which lead to Fermi-level pinning (FLP). Two approaches have been proposed to reduce the contact resistance: employing semimetal electrodes to suppress MIGS and introducing chalcogen vacancies to create non-van der Waals (non-vdW) contacts. In this work, we combine these two strategies by investigating the growth of Sn, a metallic electrode that exhibits reduced FLP and semimetal-like contact behavior on the defect-engineered WSe2, a relatively p-type TMD. Defects were introduced via ion bombardment, and the control parameters of acceleration energy and ion species (Ar+ and Ne+) were systematically studied to assess their effects on defect-creation efficiency. It is found that defect density strongly depends on the bombardment conditions, with Ne+ and lower acceleration energies leading to more efficient defect formation. Furthermore, we compared the growth behavior of Sn on defective and pristine WSe2 surfaces, and Sn islands preferentially nucleate at defect sites, indicating enhanced interaction between Sn and WSe2 due to defect-mediated nucleation. These results demonstrate that defect engineering promotes Sn nucleation and the formation of a highly covered Sn layer on WSe2, providing a structural pathway toward the realization of semimetal-like contacts with reduced contact resistance in 2D semiconductor devices.
articles.summary_en: Researchers show that ion-induced defects in WSe₂ promote tin nucleation and produce highly covered semimetal-like contact layers. Ne⁺ bombardment and lower acceleration energies generated defects more efficiently, offering a route to reduced-resistance contacts in scaled 2D semiconductor devices.

articles.title_original: Pseudomagnetic focusing of valley-polarized beams in strained graphene
articles.title_en: Strained graphene enables pseudomagnetic focusing of valley-polarized currents
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract In addition to spin, the low-energy charge carriers in graphene have two inequivalent valley flavors K and K' related by time-reversal symmetry, which can potentially serve as carriers for additional information. One promising route of controlling the valley degree of freedom relies on strain-induced pseudomagnetic fields, which couple with opposite signs to the two valleys. In this work, we theoretically investigate quantum transport in strained graphene devices that host tailored pseudomagnetic field profiles for valley manipulation. We focus on experimentally feasible geometries and propose transverse pseudomagnetic focusing in a bent graphene ribbon as an efficient method for generating valley-polarized currents, even in presence of disorder. Our work highlights pseudomagneto-transport in graphene as a viable tool for valleytronic applications.
articles.summary_en: Researchers theoretically propose using tailored strain-induced pseudomagnetic fields to focus valley-polarized charge carriers in bent graphene ribbons. The approach could support valleytronic devices and is designed to remain effective in the presence of disorder.

articles.title_original: Active tunability of simultaneous electromagnetically induced transparency and reflection in a graphene-assisted planar terahertz metasurface
articles.title_en: Graphene metasurface enables tunable terahertz transparency and reflection
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract We demonstrate actively tunable electromagnetically induced transparency (EIT) and electromagnetically induced reflection (EIR) in a planar coupled terahertz metasurface. The configuration comprises a cross resonator and two arc-shaped ring resonators placed in close proximity. The strong coupling between the resonators exhibits a transparency window in an otherwise absorptive region when placed in a near-field configuration. Passive tuning of the EIT and EIR responses is achieved by varying the resonator length, enabling precise control over the spectral characteristics of the coupled system. To achieve an actively tunable EIT and EIR effect, a monolayer of graphene is integrated to the metasurface, separated by a thin layer of flexible polyimide spacer. Variation in the Fermi energy of graphene results in active modulation of the EIT and EIR effects. A coupled oscillator theoretical model is employed to validate the simulation results and provide a deeper understanding of the coupling between the resonators. Furthermore, active modulation of the slow-light effect for both EIT and EIR effects is demonstrated. The study simultaneously demonstrates active EIT and EIR responses in the same metamaterial structure at resonance frequencies of 0.80 THz and 1.06 THz, respectively. This study also demonstrates the passive and active control of EIT and EIR effects, which can lead to the advancement of slow light devices, optical switches, and filters in the field of terahertz photonics.
articles.summary_en: Researchers demonstrated active control of electromagnetically induced transparency and reflection at 0.80 and 1.06 THz by integrating monolayer graphene into a planar metasurface. The approach could support tunable slow-light devices, optical switches, and terahertz filters, although the work remains at the research stage.

articles.title_original: Smart Mxene Enabled Marine Composite Materials for Structural Health Monitoring of Offshore Engineering Systems
articles.title_en: MXene Marine Composites Enable Integrated Offshore Structural Health Monitoring
articles.excerpt_original: Offshore structures are exposed to seawater, corrosion, cyclic loading, fatigue, and mechanical degradation, requiring durable materials with integrated structural health monitoring (SHM) capabilities for functioning effectively. Conventional SHM systems generally depend on separately mounted sensors, thereby increasing system complexity and vulnerability to harsh marine environments. This research develops a smart MXene-enabled marine composite for integrated damage and deformation monitoring of offshore engineering structures. Marine-grade epoxy polymer matrix, amine-based hardener, Ti₃C₂Tₓ MXene nanomaterial, and glass fiber reinforcement were used to fabricate smart marine composite materials for SHM, and they were characterized using scanning electron microscopy (SEM), X-ray diffraction (XRD), Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR), electrical conductivity, tensile, and piezoresistive strain-sensing tests. Saltwater immersion and cyclic loading are performed to assess marine durability and sensing stability. The composite exhibits effective MXene dispersion, conductive-network formation, repeatable resistance responses, and sensitivity to mechanical deformation and progressive damage. MXene composite achieved maximum conductivity of 3.962 S/m at 2.0 wt.% loading. Overall, MXene-enabled marine composites provide a promising approach for lightweight, durable, and integrated SHM of offshore engineering structures.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed glass-fiber-reinforced epoxy composites containing Ti₃C₂Tₓ MXene for embedded damage and deformation sensing in offshore structures. The material formed a conductive network, reaching 3.962 S/m conductivity at 2.0 wt.% MXene, while maintaining repeatable piezoresistive responses after saltwater immersion and cyclic loading.

articles.title_original: Multi Interface-Enhanced Ni(Fe)P/Ni(Fe)OOH/MXene Catalysts for Efficient Alkaline Electrolysis
articles.title_en: MXene Composite Catalyst Improves Alkaline Seawater Electrolysis
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Electrochemical water electrolysis for hydrogen production offers a feasible way for renewable energy development but still faces significant challenges. Developing high-performance catalysts with high activity, low cost, long-term stability, corrosion resistance, and antisediment aggregation is crucial for the practical application of water electrolysis, particularly seawater electrolysis. For this purpose, we designed a Ni(Fe)P/Ni(Fe)OOH/MXene composite electrocatalyst on an iron foam substrate, which uses a multi-interface structure, Fe self-doping, and incomplete phosphating to jointly adjust the electronic structure and optimize H* absorption. Importantly, the incorporation of MXene significantly enhances electrical conductivity, increases the exposure sites, and facilitates gas release, thereby boosting the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) performance. Meanwhile, the self-doping of the substrate and vertically staggered nanosheet morphology induced by MXene are utilized to enhance the bonding between the catalyst and substrate, as well as the antisediment aggregation performance, thereby achieving long-term stable operation in an alkaline seawater environment. Consequently, the catalyst demonstrates outstanding HER behavior, achieving 100 mA cm–2 at 140 mV in freshwater and 165 mV in seawater, while maintaining stability for 45 h. Moreover, Ni(Fe)P/Ni(Fe)OOH/MXene was assembled with Fe-Ni(OH)2 into a dual-electrode electrolysis cell, achieving 10 mA cm–2 at only 1.49 V in freshwater, and 1.56 V in natural seawater. This work may open up a prospect for freshwater electrolysis of high efficiency HER catalyst.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a Ni(Fe)P/Ni(Fe)OOH/MXene catalyst on iron foam for hydrogen evolution in alkaline freshwater and seawater. The catalyst reached 100 mA cm−2 at 165 mV in seawater and operated stably for 45 hours; a paired cell achieved 1.56 V at 10 mA cm−2 in natural seawater.

articles.title_original: High-Throughput In-Operando Terahertz Time-Domain Spectroscopy of Chemical Vapor Deposited Graphene for pH Sensing
articles.title_en: Contactless terahertz spectroscopy enables high-throughput pH sensing in CVD graphene
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Reliable pH sensing in liquid environments underpins applications in energy storage, biosensing, and process monitoring, yet conventional graphene-based electrical devices introduce ohmic contacts, encapsulation layers, and electrochemical artifacts that can obscure intrinsic behavior. These approaches also fail to capture the strong spatial variability of commercial CVD graphene. Here, we present a fully contactless methodology for quantifying pH-dependent conductivity of large-area CVD graphene using through-substrate reflection terahertz time-domain spectroscopy (THz-TDS). A customized liquid cell with a THz transparent window preserves unrestricted access to the graphene–electrolyte interface while enabling centimeter-scale conductivity mapping and in-operando single-point monitoring during sequential pH modulation. By integrating spatially registered Raman mapping with automated quality-metric filtering, we extract statistically robust trends across thousands of pixels rather than isolated device regions. We show that pristine monolayer graphene exhibits the highest baseline conductivity and strongest pH sensitivity, whereas O2-plasma-introduced defects systematically suppress both. This scalable, remote, and inert probing approach establishes THz-TDS as a powerful platform for high-throughput characterization and robust liquid-phase sensing in thin films and 2D systems.
articles.summary_en: Researchers demonstrate through-substrate terahertz time-domain spectroscopy for contactless, in-operando mapping of pH-dependent conductivity in large-area CVD graphene. Pristine monolayer graphene showed the strongest pH sensitivity, while plasma-induced defects reduced conductivity and response, supporting scalable liquid-phase sensing and materials characterization.

articles.title_original: Thermally driven oxidation and conductive-to-insulating transition of liquid-metal-printed gallium films for 2D electronics
articles.title_en: Thermal oxidation converts printed gallium films into 2D-electronics dielectrics
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Liquid-metal-derived oxide nanofilms have emerged as promising candidates for scalable electronic materials, yet the oxidation pathway governing their electrical functionality remains poorly understood. Here, we report a systematic study on the thermally driven oxidation behavior of liquid-metal-printed gallium films and its decisive role in inducing a conductive-toinsulating transition for two-dimensional (2D) electronics. Ultrathin gallium-based films were prepared through a dewetting-enabled printing process under ambient conditions, yielding smooth and transferable films with single-layer thicknesses of ~4.5 nm. The as-printed films exhibit partial surface oxidation while retaining residual metallic gallium, resulting in conductive vertical transport. Pure oxygen exposure at room temperature leads mainly to surface adsorption of oxygen species and fails to achieve complete oxidation. In contrast, thermal annealing in oxygen-containing atmosphere progressively converts metallic Ga into gallium oxide, as evidenced by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy. High-temperature treatment further induces crystallization into polycrystalline β-Ga 2 O 3 , confirmed by X-ray diffraction and Raman spectroscopy. Consequently, the printed films undergo a pronounced conductive-to-insulating transition, exhibiting pA-level leakage current, and a dielectric constant of ~4.2. When integrated as gate dielectrics in back-gated MoS 2 field-effect transistors, the devices deliver an on/off ratio of ~10 6 and a minimum subthreshold swing of 74 mV/dec. This work clarifies the thermal oxidation mechanism of liquid-metal-printed gallium films and establishes a scalable route toward functional dielectric layers for next-generation 2D electronics.
articles.summary_en: Researchers showed that oxygen annealing transforms ultrathin liquid-metal-printed gallium films into crystalline gallium oxide, driving a conductive-to-insulating transition. Integrated as gate dielectrics in MoS₂ transistors, the films achieved an on/off ratio of approximately 10⁶ and a minimum subthreshold swing of 74 mV/dec.

articles.title_original: Synergistic regulation of point defect and uniaxial strain on the adsorption of methane on graphene: First-principles study
articles.title_en: Defect–strain engineering improves methane adsorption on graphene
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Based on first-principles calculations, we systematically investigate the synergistic influence of point defects (Stone-Wales and double vacancy) and uniaxial strain on the adsorption of methane (CH 4 ) on graphene. For the SWG/CH 4 system, the SW defect enhances CH 4 adsorption capacity, whereas the adsorption energy remains nearly insensitive to uniaxial strain, exhibiting isotropic strain dependence. For the DVG555-777/CH 4 system, compressive strain plays a dominant role, driving a physisorption-to-chemisorption transition and exhibiting pronounced anisotropy. The defect and strain synergy also significantly tunes the electronic structure, tensile strain reduces the pseudogap of DVG555-777/CH 4 and induces magnetism in a strain-direction and magnitude-dependent manner, notably, a 3% strain along the AM direction generates a magnetic moment of 0.122µB, predominantly from C atom p z orbital electrons, offering a magnetically-based CH 4 detection approach. Moreover, the cooperative effect of the double vacancy defect and uniaxial compressive strain effectively weakens the CH 4 -substrate interaction, enabling experimentally observable recovery times at room temperature. These findings propose a promising defect-strain synergistic strategy for designing highly sensitive CH 4 sensors with rapid recovery.
articles.summary_en: First-principles calculations show that combining graphene defects with uniaxial strain can tune methane adsorption, electronic structure, and magnetic response. The findings suggest a route to sensitive, rapidly recovering graphene-based methane sensors, though experimental validation is still needed.

articles.title_original: Tailoring thermo-mechanical and optoelectronic properties in Janus Hf2CClBr and Hf2CClI MXenes: A DFT study
articles.title_en: DFT study maps thermo-mechanical and optoelectronic properties of Janus Hf₂CClBr and Hf₂CClI MXenes
articles.excerpt_original: In this study, first-principles calculations are performed to investigate the phase stability and the mechanical, thermal, and optoelectronic properties of the Janus MXenes Hf 2 CClBr and Hf 2 CClI. The thermodynamic and dynamical stabilities of these compounds are evaluated using formation energy calculations and phonon dispersion spectra, revealing that both structures are stable. Mechanical stability is verified by analyzing the elastic stiffness constants, which confirm that the investigated Janus MXenes are mechanically stable. In addition, the evaluated Pugh’s and Poisson’s ratios reveal that Hf 2 CClBr behaves as a ductile material, while Hf 2 CClI exhibits brittle characteristics. The metallic characteristics of the materials investigated are primarily attributed to the Hf- 5d orbitals. The major contribution of Hf-5d orbitals at the Fermi level is 78 % and 72 % of the total density of states for Hf 2 CClBr and Hf 2 CClI, respectively. Moreover, a comprehensive analysis of the optical properties has been conducted to evaluate the response of Hf 2 CClBr and Hf 2 CClI to incident electromagnetic waves. The results reveal a pronounced absorption peak in the energy range of approximately 8-9 eV and a maximum reflectivity above 80 % in the IR region and ∼70-80% in the visible region up to 2.1 eV. These distinctive optical characteristics highlight the potential of these materials for various optoelectronic and technological applications. Lattice-sheet conductance and sheet resistance have been calculated and discussed. The calculated ultra-low thermal sheet conductance of Hf 2 CClBr and Hf 2 CClI at 300 K is 4.05 nW K -1 and 4.71 nW K -1 , respectively. articles.summary_en: First-principles calculations indicate that both Janus MXenes are thermodynamically, dynamically, and mechanically stable, with contrasting ductile and brittle behavior. Their high infrared and visible reflectivity, alongside ultra-low calculated thermal sheet conductance at 300 K, suggests potential for optoelectronic and thermal-management applications.

articles.title_original: Low‐Flicker‐Noise MoS 2 Transistors Enabled by High‐ κ Rare‐Earth Oxychlorides for Mixed‐Signal Electronics
articles.title_en: Rare-Earth Oxychloride Dielectrics Reduce MoS₂ Transistor Noise
articles.excerpt_original: ABSTRACT The trade‐off between gate dielectric constant and interface quality limits two‐dimensional (2D) analog and mixed‐signal electronics because trap‐mediated 1/ f noise from amorphous oxides degrades signal fidelity. Here, single‐crystalline rare‐earth oxychlorides (REOCl; LaOCl and GdOCl) are employed as Cl‐terminated crystalline high‐ κ dielectrics that form atomically abrupt van der Waals interfaces with MoS 2 . MoS 2 /REOCl transistors exhibit near‐thermal‐limit switching, with minimum one‐decade‐averaged subthreshold swings of 65.7 and 63.2 mV dec −1 for LaOCl and GdOCl, with ultralow hysteresis and suppressed low‐frequency noise. Carrier‐number‐fluctuation analysis of two independently measured devices per dielectric yields effective noise‐derived interface trap densities of 1.15–1.94 × 10 10 cm −2 eV −1 , approaching the hexagonal boron nitride regime while retaining high‐ κ electrostatic coupling. Channel‐area‐scaled normalized 1/ f noise remains up to two orders of magnitude below amorphous SiO 2 /Al 2 O 3 /HfO 2 controls, with on‐state S I / I D 2 reaching ∼10 −10 Hz −1 . A Samsung 28 nm high‐ κ /metal‐gate reference process design kit sensitivity analysis, with only the flicker‐noise coefficient varied, indicates reduced voltage‐controlled oscillator phase noise and phase‐locked‐loop jitter and an effective‐number‐of‐bits improvement of up to 1.45 bits in passive noise‐shaping successive‐approximation‐register analog‐to‐digital converters. These results establish REOCl as a trap‐poor high‐ κ dielectric platform for low‐noise 2D electronics and illustrate the mixed‐signal relevance of reduced transistor flicker noise.
articles.summary_en: Researchers demonstrated MoS₂ transistors using crystalline LaOCl and GdOCl high-κ dielectrics, achieving near-thermal-limit switching and flicker noise up to two orders of magnitude below conventional oxide controls. Modeling indicates potential gains in oscillator, phase-locked-loop, and analog-to-digital converter performance for mixed-signal electronics.

articles.title_original: Programmable Integration of Metal–Sulfur Coordination Motifs Into Layered Lead Halides for Photocatalytic CO 2 Reduction
articles.title_en: Layered Lead Halides Integrate Metal–Sulfur Catalysts for CO₂ Conversion
articles.excerpt_original: ABSTRACT Two‐dimensional (2D) lead halides provide a versatile platform for interlayer engineering, but their functionality is limited by electronically inert spacers. The integration of electronically active inorganic motifs into layered lead halide lattices remains a major challenge. Herein, we report a coordination‐directed strategy that enables the programmable incorporation of transition‐metal–sulfur (MS 2 ) units into layered lead halides via synergistic carboxylate‐sulfide dual binding, affording a family of 12 crystalline frameworks with tunable compositions. Embedding electronically and catalytically active MS 2 motifs transforms the interlayer region from a passive dielectric component into an active domain for charge transport and catalysis. Notably, CoS 2 ‐ and NiS 2 ‐intercalated lead–halide materials exhibit efficient CO 2 ‐to‐CO conversion, achieving rates up to 4.32 mmol g −1 h −1 , an apparent quantum yield of 1.76%, and near‐unity selectivity. Combined in situ spectroscopy and density functional theory calculations identify NiS 2 as the optimal catalytic center, featuring favorable band alignment, efficient charge transfer, and moderate CO adsorption. In contrast, the FeS 2 ‐intercalated material suffers from catalyst poisoning due to strong CO binding, while MnS 2 ‐, ZnS 2 ‐, and CuS 2 ‐based systems are limited by unfavorable energy alignment with the photosensitizer or competing self‐reduction pathways. This work introduces a new paradigm that integrates efficient light‐harvesting, charge transport, and catalytic functionality within a single layered semiconductor.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed 12 layered lead-halide frameworks incorporating transition-metal–sulfur motifs as active interlayer domains. CoS₂- and NiS₂-containing materials enabled selective CO₂-to-CO photocatalysis, with NiS₂ delivering the strongest charge-transfer and catalytic performance.

articles.title_original: Recent progress of the exchange bias based on 2D van der Waals ferromagnet
articles.title_en: Review Advances Exchange Bias in 2D van der Waals Ferromagnets
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Exchange bias (EB) is a central mechanism in spintronics, enabling unidirectional magnetic anisotropy, enhanced coercivity, and stable pinned magnetic states through interfacial exchange coupling. Two‐dimensional (2D) van der Waals (vdW) magnets offer a new platform for engineering EB at the atomic scale, where sharp interfaces, reduced dimensionality, tunable interlayer coupling, and strong magnetic anisotropy give rise to unconventional interfacial spin phenomena. This review summarizes the recent progress in EB in 2D vdW magnetic heterostructures. We discuss the fundamental principles, key parameters, and theoretical models of EB followed by representative vdW systems based primarily on ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic materials. Particular attention is given to interfacial mechanisms including uncompensated spins, oxidation‐induced pinning, charge transfer, magnetic proximity effects, and spin–orbit coupling. We further examine external control strategies such as electric‐field tuning, thermal modulation, optical excitation, and strain engineering, as well as emerging applications in field‐free spin–orbit‐torque switching, magnetic tunnel junctions, spin‐filter devices, and nonvolatile memories. Finally, we outline the key challenges of thermal stability, interface reproducibility, and scalable fabrication. This review provides a compact framework for understanding and designing EB in 2D vdW heterostructures for future spintronic and quantum‐enabled technologies.
articles.summary_en: This review examines exchange bias in 2D van der Waals magnetic heterostructures, focusing on interfacial spin mechanisms and control through electric fields, heat, light, and strain. It highlights potential applications in spin–orbit-torque switching, magnetic tunnel junctions, spin filters, and nonvolatile memory, while noting challenges in stability, reproducibility, and scalable fabrication.

articles.excerpt_original: In this study, nano-hexagonal boron nitride (hBN), dispersant gum arabic (GA) and dispersant cetyltrimeth-ylammonium bromide (CTAB) were added in different proportions and concentrations in cooling water (coolant). The fixed concentration of nano-hexagonal boron nitride is 0.75 wt.%, and the weight ratio of nano-hexagonal boron nitride to dispersant CTAB is 3:2 to make S1, the weight ratio to dispersant GA is 1:1 to make S2, and the weight ratio to dispersant GA is 2:1 to make S3, as well as three hexagonal boron nitride nano-coolants (hBNNC) with different concentrations were compared with the coolant for basic tests. The basic tests can be divided into: settlement, heat conduction, viscosity, specific heat and friction tests. The performance of the coolant is optimized by adding nano-hBN and dispersant, and then the cooling state of the actual application of electric motorcycles is simulated through the heat exchange platform to verify the optimization results. According to the results, in the basic test, S2 showed better results compared to the coolant, S1 and S3. In the heat exchange platform test, compared to the coolant, S2 had a patent effect and could quickly drop to room temperature at high temperatures.
articles.summary_en: Researchers tested hBN nanocoolants with gum arabic or CTAB dispersants across settling, thermal conductivity, viscosity, specific heat, friction, and heat exchange. The S2 formulation using gum arabic at a 1:1 hBN-to-dispersant ratio showed the strongest performance and rapidly reduced high temperatures to room temperature in simulated electric-motorcycle cooling tests.

articles.title_original: Molecular Bridges for 2D Nanomaterials
articles.title_en: Molecular Bridges Proposed to Engineer 2D Material Interfaces
articles.excerpt_original: ABSTRACT The exceptional electronic, optical, and chemical properties of nanomaterials are often compromised when individual building blocks are assembled into macroscopic devices, where poorly defined interfaces govern charge transport, mechanical integrity, and functional performance. Cross‐linking has emerged as a powerful strategy for engineering these interfaces by introducing molecular bridges that couple neighboring nanostructures and control their structural and electronic interactions. Although this concept has been explored in nanoparticle assemblies, its translation to 2D materials remains in its early stages. In this perspective, we propose molecular cross‐linking as a unifying framework for interfacial engineering across nanomaterial systems, highlighting how linker chemistry governs spacing between nanomaterials, charge transport, mechanical behavior, and chemical functionality. By comparing molecular bridging strategies in metal nanoparticles, quantum dots, transition‐metal dichalcogenides, graphene oxide, and MXenes, we review how different binding motifs and types of linkers give rise to distinct structure‐property relationships. Building on our recent demonstration of hydrogen‐bonded diamine bridging in Ti 3 C 2 T x MXenes, we propose molecular junction engineering as a general design principle for 2D materials. We envision that a programmable molecular interface will enable next‐generation hybrid materials with tunable charge‐transport characteristics, mechanics, and chemical functionality, extending far beyond MXenes to a broad class of molecularly engineered 2D systems.
articles.summary_en: The perspective examines molecular cross-linking as a strategy to control spacing, charge transport, mechanical integrity, and chemical functionality in assembled 2D nanomaterials, including graphene oxide and MXenes. It proposes programmable molecular junctions as a broader design principle for hybrid materials, but reports no specific commercial application or company involvement.

articles.title_original: Review of Graphene Liquid Cell (In Situ TEM) for Battery Materials
articles.title_en: Review examines graphene liquid-cell TEM for battery materials
articles.excerpt_original: ABSTRACT The rapid development in power generation from renewable energy sources has led to the increased need for energy storage systems such as batteries, supercapacitors, and fuel cells. Consequently, extensive research and development are being conducted globally on these systems. However, to ensure the efficient performance of the energy storage systems, it is necessary to understand their associated complex electrochemical reactions and their failure mechanisms. In situ observation by liquid‐cell transmission electron microscopy (in situ TEM) has recently attracted significant attention from researchers as a material characterization technique. It allows observation and visualization of materials in liquid‐phase samples without the need to freeze or dry, which opens up the opportunity to analyze the materials in real time. In this review, we provide a comprehensive review of the recent application of in situ TEM in the characterization of energy storage materials using graphene liquid cells. We first describe the different steps and procedures involved in graphene liquid cell in situ TEM sample characterization, including sample preparation and probing, and how data are analyzed. We also discuss the challenges, opportunities, and future perspectives of the in situ graphene liquid‐cell TEM applications in energy storage systems.
articles.summary_en: A review surveys graphene liquid-cell in situ TEM as a method for observing electrochemical reactions and failure mechanisms in energy-storage materials in real time. It covers sample preparation, analysis workflows, current challenges, and future opportunities, positioning the technique as a characterization tool rather than a battery technology itself.

articles.title_original: Electron beam-induced p -to- n conversion and enhanced carrier injection in suspended GaSe devices
articles.title_en: Electron irradiation converts p-type GaSe devices to n-type
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Electron beam irradiation offers a route for carrier-type control in two-dimensional semiconductors. We fabricated a suspended p -type gallium selenide (GaSe) device and measured its electrical transport using in-situ transmission electron microscopy. Focused electron beam irradiation of the GaSe channel increased current from the nanoampere to the microampere range. Gate-dependent measurements revealed conversion from p -type to n -type conduction, accompanied by an increase in electron density. The increased electron density is expected to narrow the depletion region at the Au/GaSe interfaces, producing nearly linear current–voltage characteristics. These results demonstrate local control of carrier type and density in GaSe devices.
articles.summary_en: Researchers demonstrated that focused electron-beam irradiation converts suspended p-type gallium selenide (GaSe) devices to n-type conduction while increasing electron density and current. The technique enables local control of carrier type and improves carrier injection at Au/GaSe interfaces, potentially supporting tunable two-dimensional semiconductor devices.

articles.title_original: Surface reconstruction governs graphene epitaxy on sapphire
articles.title_en: Surface Reconstruction Controls Graphene Epitaxy on Sapphire
articles.excerpt_original: The direct growth of single-crystal graphene on dielectric substrates is highly appealing for semiconductor technologies, particularly in optoelectronics. Sapphire (α- Al 2 O 3 (0001), c-plane) is a platform holding great promise, yet graphene growth on this surface remains poorly understood and often results in rotational disorder and mosaicity. A key source of ambiguity is that the role of the surface reconstruction, ubiquitous under growth conditions, is often overlooked. In this work, we provide experimental and theoretical results that clearly indicate how graphene epitaxy on sapphire is governed by the reconstructed interface. Specifically, we show that two low-strain commensurate configurations of graphene on the most stable surface reconstruction under growth conditions, the (√31×√31)R±9°, account for the majority of experimentally observed domains. We further suggest an alternative interpretation in which the frequently observed R30 orientation may emerge from the convolution of nearby commensurate domains, yielding a unified picture of graphene growth on sapphire. Our results highlight interface control as the key requirement for achieving flat, strain-free graphene with epitaxially constrained orientations on sapphire, and establish a consistent framework to interpret the observed graphene aligned R30 with respect to the sapphire (1×1), as well as its distributed mosaicity.
articles.summary_en: Experimental and theoretical research finds that reconstructed sapphire interfaces govern graphene’s epitaxial orientations and help explain observed rotational disorder. The findings identify interface control as important for producing flat, low-strain graphene on sapphire, with implications for semiconductor and optoelectronic applications.

articles.title_original: Electronic opacity in double bilayer graphene junctions
articles.title_en: Fano interference controls electron transmission in double bilayer graphene
articles.excerpt_original: In this paper, we examine the transmission probability through a symmetric double bilayer-graphene junction modulated by Fano-type interference. At oblique incidence, two trajectories generated by Fano resonances and a quasi-bound well state are combined to generate perfect Fano interference resulting in null electron transmission. Interestingly, the transmission can be changed between normal and anomalous simply by adjusting the relative phase of the Fano resonances due to the appropriate modulation of the incidence angle, height of potential, and barrier and well width. This phenomenon is similar to electromagnetically induced absorption or to phase control of light propagation in quantum wells via Fano interference.
articles.summary_en: Researchers analyze how Fano-type interference modulates electron transmission through symmetric double bilayer graphene junctions. Adjusting incidence angle, potential height, and barrier or well widths can switch transmission between normal and anomalous regimes, including complete suppression of transmission.

articles.title_original: Time-Reversal Symmetry in Artificial Topological Graphene Rings
articles.title_en: Time-Reversal Symmetry in Artificial Topological Graphene Rings
articles.excerpt_original: We study an artificial graphene ring described by the low-energy two-valley Dirac Hamiltonian with a uniform mass term. When the ring is threaded by an Aharonov-Bohm flux, the problem reduces to a second-order radial equation solved by Bessel functions. We give the exact secular equation and, for narrow rings, closed expressions for the spectrum and the persistent current. We then add a uniform magnetic field perpendicular to the plane. The radial problem is solved with confluent hypergeometric functions, and the persistent current and magnetization are written as derivatives of a secular determinant from which the spurious roots have been removed. Besides the usual orbital coupling, the field enters through a valley-dependent term that comes from the Dirac structure and lifts the valley degeneracy. A weak-field expansion, accurate up to corrections of order B^4, gives this valley splitting explicitly and separates the diamagnetic and paramagnetic contributions to the susceptibility. Finally, we work out what time reversal implies for the spectrum. Physical time reversal, which exchanges the valleys, leads to an exact relation between levels at opposite fields. The effective single-valley time reversal, on the other hand, is broken by the mass term and by the boundary conditions, yet leaves no trace in the zero-field spectrum. Numerical results for the spectrum, the persistent current, and the magnetization illustrate the analysis.
articles.summary_en: Researchers derive exact and approximate expressions for the spectrum, persistent current, magnetization, and susceptibility of artificial graphene rings under Aharonov–Bohm flux and perpendicular magnetic fields. The study shows how valley-dependent magnetic coupling and mass or boundary conditions affect time-reversal symmetry and valley degeneracy.

articles.title_original: Regulating MXene Interlayer Chemistry: A Facile Vapor-Phase Sulfurization Strategy for Enhanced Lithium Storage
articles.title_en: Vapor-Phase Sulfurization Improves MXene Lithium Storage
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract MXene-based materials are promising anodes for lithium-ion batteries due to their metallic conductivity and layered structures. However, conventional surface terminations create heterogeneous interlayer chemistry, causing uneven charge distribution, sluggish Li+ transport, and inefficient utilization of active sites. Herein, we report a vapor-phase sulfurization strategy to construct sulfur-modulated layered materials from MAX precursors. Sulfur incorporation modulates the local electronic environment, enhancing electronic coupling and Li+ migration pathways. Density functional theory calculations reveal increased electronic states near the Fermi level, reduced charge localization, and lower Li+ diffusion barriers compared with Ti3C2Tx MXene. Consequently, Li+ storage in sulfur-modulated S–Ti3C2 involves both interlayer insertion and sulfur-related Faradaic reactions, delivering a reversible capacity of 955 mAh g–1, approximately 2.6 times that of conventional HF-etched Ti3C2Tx. This work demonstrates that vapor-phase sulfurization provides an effective route for regulating the electronic structure and charge-storage chemistry of MAX-derived layered materials.
articles.summary_en: Researchers report a vapor-phase sulfurization method that modifies MXene interlayer chemistry and improves lithium-ion transport. The sulfur-modulated material achieved a reversible capacity of 955 mAh g−1, about 2.6 times that of conventionally etched Ti3C2Tx MXene.

articles.title_original: Nonlinear Optical Absorption in 2D MXene Based Materials via Oxidation Engineering
articles.title_en: Oxidation Engineering Tunes MXene Nonlinear Optical Absorption
articles.excerpt_original: As a rapidly expanding family of 2D materials, MXenes have attracted considerable interest for photonic applications, and their oxide derivatives offer an additional degree of freedom for tailoring their optical responses. Here, we systematically investigate how controlled oxidation regulates the nonlinear optical absorption (NOA) of Ti3C2Tx MXene. The MXene films are prepared using a transfer-free, layer-by-layer self-assembly method, followed by conversion into MXene oxide (MXO) and TiO2 through a two-step oxidation process. The NOA behaviors of the MXene and corresponding MXO and TiO2 derivatives are characterized by Z-scan measurements at ~515, ~800, and ~1030 nm, showing distinct wavelength-dependent responses. All three materials exhibit reverse saturable absorption (RSA) at ~800 nm, and progressive oxidation induces saturable absorption (SA)-to-RSA transitions at ~515 and ~1030 nm. This transition is particularly notable at ~1030 nm, where the nonlinear absorption coefficient β changes from ~−9.05 × 10−10 m/W for MXene to ~2.07 × 10−9 m/W for TiO2. Intensity-dependent measurements further reveal distinct variations in β among the three materials. These results establish controlled oxidation as an effective strategy for engineering the NOA of MXene-derived materials and provide insight into the evolution of their nonlinear optical properties, offering a versatile material platform for potential nonlinear optical applications such as optical modulation and optical limiting.
articles.summary_en: Researchers show that controlled oxidation of Ti3C2Tx MXene systematically changes its nonlinear optical absorption, including wavelength-dependent shifts between saturable and reverse saturable absorption. The findings support MXene-derived oxides as candidate materials for optical modulation and limiting applications.

articles.title_original: Conformal MXene surface engineering enables ultra-low-energy fibre-laser powder bed fusion of PEEK composites
articles.title_en: MXene-Coated PEEK Enables Ultra-Low-Energy Laser Powder Bed Fusion
articles.excerpt_original: Polyetheretherketone (PEEK) is attractive for patient-specific load-bearing implants, but its low absorption at near-infrared radiation (NIR) fibre-laser wavelengths and narrow processing window make powder bed fusion challenging. Here, Ti3C2Tx MXene nanosheets were conformally assembled on PEEK particles by electrostatic adsorption to construct Ti3C2Tx-sheathed powders with improved NIR absorption, heat transfer, and flowability. The modified powders enable stable multilayer fibre-laser powder bed fusion (f-LPBF) at ultralow volume energy densities. For PEEK/M1, the required energy density was reduced from 26.667 to 0.333 J⊕mm−3, representing a 98.75% reduction relative to pristine PEEK, while maintaining a slightly expander processable window and suppressing carbonisation-induced instability. The printed S-PEEK/M1 composites showed enhanced interlayer fusion, smoother surfaces, increased crystallinity, and a transcrystalline microstructure, resulting in a tensile strength of 71.71 ± 5.06 MPa, a flexural strength of 87.35 ± 8.02 MPa, and a Vickers hardness of 39.78 ± 3.22 HV. This work demonstrates a powder-level MXene engineering route that couples optical-thermal processability with mechanical reinforcement, providing a general strategy for high-throughput f-LPBF of high-performance polymer composites for biomedical and engineering applications.
articles.summary_en: Researchers engineered PEEK particles with conformal Ti3C2Tx MXene coatings, improving near-infrared absorption, heat transfer, and powder flowability. The approach reduced required fusion energy density by 98.75% while preserving mechanical performance, supporting patient-specific biomedical implants and other high-performance polymer applications.
